1The question

What can local measurements reconstruct?

A field theory assigns measurements to regions of space. When two regions are disjoint, their measurements can be combined. When the regions meet, the combined measurement can acquire singular terms. The problem of this programme is to recover algebraic and geometric structures from those products, while retaining the information carried by the singularities. Its central questions concern the passage from an associative algebra to a second associative algebra, the symmetries of the resulting fields, and the recovery of a bulk theory from measurements on a boundary.

An observable is a quantity associated to fields in a specified region: classically a function of those fields, and after quantization an element of the algebra of measurements. An operator field packages a family of such operators depending on an insertion point. In a local complex coordinate, we write it as J(z)J(z).

The simplest example already contains the difficulty. Two copies of a current can have the product

J(z)J(w)∼κ(z−w)2𝟏. J(z)J(w)\sim \frac{\kappa}{(z-w)^2}\,\mathbf1.

Here κ\kappa is a scalar, 𝟏\mathbf1 is the identity insertion, and ∼\sim records only the singular part as zz approaches ww. The product has a double pole. Its coefficient survives even when the fields have zero expectation individually. A record of products that forgets their singular expansion, or keeps only the regular value at coincidence, loses the vacuum contribution in this equation.

A local vacuum is the distinguished identity state 𝟏\mathbf1 at a nonempty insertion. In a state–field description, its field acts as the identity, and applying any field to 𝟏\mathbf1 creates the translated state. A prepared state instead supplies an evaluation of observables, such as a linear functional λ\lambda determined by boundary data. Its associated correlation function is the evaluation of a product of insertions; in a vacuum representation it has the form λ(J(z1)⋯J(zn)𝟏)\lambda(J(z_1)\cdots J(z_n)\mathbf1).

The identity insertion and the evaluating functional therefore answer different questions. The first specifies how a field acts when an insertion is empty of excitation. The second assigns a number to the resulting state. Even the existence of a suitable algebra of fields does not choose its evaluating functional, its integration cycle, or its positivity properties. A reconstruction that determines the algebra but leaves these choices open has made a definite advance without yet determining the physical correlation functions.

There are also two different ways to combine insertions. We may bring points together in the complex direction, where the poles above matter. In a theory with an additional real direction, we may compose measurements along an interval. These operations must agree on configurations where both can be performed. Establishing each operation separately does not establish that agreement. The relevant comparison must retain the terms supported where insertions collide.

The basic examples make these requirements concrete. The single current above detects the distinction between a vacuum and a scalar evaluation. Several currents add a Lie bracket to the double pole. Charged exponential fields introduce signs and continuation around a collision. Free fields with an asymmetric contraction distinguish exchanging insertions from merely multiplying them. Together they explain why the geometric definitions below retain positions, orders, collisions, units and the precise coefficient spaces.

The account then follows the reconstruction in both directions. Starting from fields, it organizes their collision coefficients and forms an associative algebra of operations. Starting from suitable algebraic data, it constructs a second algebra and asks whether that algebra can again be expressed by states and fields. Several such constructions are proved on their stated domains. Their comparisons remain the decisive questions: which operations survive, which require a different domain, and which are ruled out by an explicit example?

2Basic examples

One current, and the information in its pole

Work over a characteristic-zero field kk; analytic continuation below uses k=ℂk=\mathbb C. Write the current as J(z)=∑n∈ℤJnz−n−1J(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}J_nz^{-n-1}. The residue of a Laurent differential f(u)duf(u)\,du at u=0u=0 is the coefficient of u−1duu^{-1}du. Taking the residues of the double pole in the two insertion variables gives

[Jm,Jn]=κmδm+n,01.[J_m,J_n]=\kappa m\,\delta_{m+n,0}\,1.

Indeed, the residue in zz of zmκ/(z−w)2z^m\kappa/(z-w)^2 is κmwm−1\kappa m w^{m-1}; taking the residue against wndww^n\,dw gives the displayed coefficient. Thus the pole determines the commutator of operators acting on states.

The Heisenberg algebra is the algebra generated by 11 and the modes JnJ_n, subject to these commutator relations. The scalar κ\kappa is its level. Its vacuum Fock space is the polynomial space Vκ=k[x1,x2,…]V_\kappa=k[x_1,x_2,\ldots], where every polynomial uses finitely many variables, with

J−n=xn,Jn=κn∂xn(n>0),J0=0,𝟏=1.J_{-n}=x_n,\qquad J_n=\kappa n\partial_{x_n}\quad(n>0),\qquad J_0=0,\qquad\mathbf1=1.

Translation acts by Txn=nxn+1Tx_n=nx_{n+1} and the product rule. In particular, [J1,J−1]𝟏=κ𝟏[J_1,J_{-1}]\mathbf1=\kappa\mathbf1.

At nonzero level, no homomorphism from this unital mode algebra to kk can preserve the scalar identity: applying it to [J1,J−1]=κ1[J_1,J_{-1}]=\kappa1 would give 0=κ0=\kappa. This is the first reason to distinguish the local vacuum from a scalar character. The linear functional that extracts a polynomial’s constant term still exists. It is an evaluation of states; it is not a character of the operator algebra.

An augmentation of a unital algebra AA over kk is an algebra homomorphism ϵ:A→k\epsilon:A\to k with ϵ(1)=1\epsilon(1)=1. Its kernel is the augmentation ideal. The polynomial state space has its ordinary constant-term augmentation as a commutative polynomial algebra. At nonzero Heisenberg level that map does not preserve the singular field products or the mode-algebra action.

This distinction persists after passing to more general coefficients. One can augment an algebra of geometric operations at the empty configuration while retaining a nonzero vacuum at every nonempty insertion. The two maps have different sources and different compatibility requirements.

Fields, translation and exchange

The modes above are the coefficients of fields. The notation also records which infinite expressions are admitted. A formal series is used through its coefficients and the operations defined on them; no numerical convergence is asserted. In V((z))V((z)) each vector-valued Laurent series has a finite lower bound on its powers of zz. The bound can depend on the input state.

A vertex algebra consists of a state space VV, a vacuum 𝟏\mathbf1, translation TT, and bilinear fields Y(a,z)b∈V((z))Y(a,z)b\in V((z)). The mode convention for every state is Y(a,z)=∑n∈ℤa(n)z−n−1Y(a,z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}a_{(n)}z^{-n-1}, so a(n)ba_{(n)}b is the coefficient of z−n−1z^{-n-1}. The axioms are T𝟏=0T\mathbf1=0, Y(𝟏,z)=idY(\mathbf1,z)=\mathrm{id}, Y(a,z)𝟏=ezTaY(a,z)\mathbf1=e^{zT}a, and [T,Y(a,z)]=Y(Ta,z)=∂zY(a,z)[T,Y(a,z)]=Y(Ta,z)=\partial_zY(a,z). Weak associativity says that, on each fixed triple of states, the expansions of Y(a,u+w)Y(b,w)cY(a,u+w)Y(b,w)c and Y(Y(a,u)b,w)cY(Y(a,u)b,w)c agree after multiplication by a sufficient power of u+wu+w. Locality says that a sufficient power of z−wz-w kills the commutator of two fields. For odd states the commutator has the corresponding parity sign.

The current state is J=J−1𝟏=x1J=J_{-1}\mathbf1=x_1, and its field is Y(J,z)=J(z)Y(J,z)=J(z); hence J(n)=JnJ_{(n)}=J_n. The polynomial descendants determine the other fields. Normal ordering places creation modes to the left of annihilation modes; their commutators supply the contractions omitted by that rearrangement. It is therefore an operation determined by the chosen mode decomposition, not ordinary multiplication of operator-valued functions at a singular point.

To state exchange relations, one must keep the two inputs independent. The tensor product V⊗RWV\otimes_R W over a commutative ring RR represents bilinear maps from V×WV\times W that balance the two RR-actions. A flat RR-module is one for which tensoring preserves exact sequences. Unless a topology is specified, the tensor product here is algebraic: its elements are finite sums of elementary tensors.

A quantum vertex algebra replaces ordinary locality by an exchange rule: reversing two insertions applies a specified operator 𝒮(z)\mathcal S(z) to their states. Subscripts such as 𝒮13\mathcal S_{13} mean that it acts on the first and third factors and leaves the second fixed. The following definition fixes the coefficient ring, the Laurent condition and the compatibility with products. The vacuum, translation and weak-associativity axioms referred to in it are the ones just stated.

Definition

A field algebra with rational exchange

Here RR is a commutative coefficient ring over a characteristic-zero field, V((u))V((u)) consists of Laurent series with finitely many negative powers on each input, and tensor products are over RR. The preceding paragraph specifies the vacuum, translation and weak-associativity axioms. The exchange acts on the indicated tensor factors; all ordered expansions in the displayed identities are part of the definition.

A quantum vertex algebra with rational exchange over 𝖱\mathsf R consists of the following data.

  1. A flat 𝖱\mathsf R-module VV with a vector 𝟏\mathbf1 spanning a free direct summand, and an operator TT.

  2. Fields Y(a,u)b∈V((u))Y(a,u)b\in V((u)), bilinear over 𝖱\mathsf R, with the vacuum and translation axioms and the weak associativity stated above.

  3. An 𝖱[z,z−1]\mathsf R[z,z^{-1}]-linear automorphism 𝒮(z)\mathcal S(z) of V⊗𝖱V⊗𝖱𝖱[z,z−1]V\otimes_{\mathsf R}V\otimes_{\mathsf R}\mathsf R[z,z^{-1}], the exchange. It fixes 𝟏⊗a\mathbf1\otimes a and a⊗𝟏a\otimes\mathbf1 for every aa.

The exchange satisfies (Sh)[T⊗1,𝒮(z)]=−∂z𝒮(z),(YB)𝒮12(z1−z2)𝒮13(z1−z3)𝒮23(z2−z3)=𝒮23(z2−z3)𝒮13(z1−z3)𝒮12(z1−z2),(U)𝒮21(−z)𝒮(z)=1.\begin{align*} &\text{(Sh)}\quad [T\otimes1,\mathcal S(z)]=-\partial_z\mathcal S(z),\\ &\text{(YB)}\quad \mathcal S_{12}(z_1-z_2)\,\mathcal S_{13}(z_1-z_3)\, \mathcal S_{23}(z_2-z_3) =\mathcal S_{23}(z_2-z_3)\,\mathcal S_{13}(z_1-z_3)\, \mathcal S_{12}(z_1-z_2),\\ &\text{(U)}\quad \mathcal S_{21}(-z)\,\mathcal S(z)=1 . \end{align*} The fields are 𝒮\mathcal S-local. For all a,ba,b there is NN such that (z1−z2)N𝒮(z1−z2)(a⊗b)(z_1-z_2)^N\mathcal S(z_1-z_2)(a\otimes b) is a polynomial in z1−z2z_1-z_2 and, for every cc, (z1−z2)NY(b,z2)Y(a,z1)c=(z1−z2)NY(z1)(1⊗Y(z2))(𝒮(z1−z2)(a⊗b)⊗c)\begin{equation} (z_1-z_2)^N\,Y(b,z_2)Y(a,z_1)c =(z_1-z_2)^N\,Y(z_1)\bigl(1\otimes Y(z_2)\bigr) \bigl(\mathcal S(z_1-z_2)(a\otimes b)\otimes c\bigr) \end{equation} as formal series in z1±1,z2±1z_1^{\pm1},z_2^{\pm1}. Exchange and fields satisfy the hexagon (H)𝒮(z)(Y(w)⊗1)=(Y(w)⊗1)𝒮23(z)𝒮13(z+w).\begin{equation} \text{(H)}\quad \mathcal S(z)\bigl(Y(w)\otimes1\bigr) =\bigl(Y(w)\otimes1\bigr)\,\mathcal S_{23}(z)\,\mathcal S_{13}(z+w). \end{equation} It is an identity of maps from V⊗3V^{\otimes3} to (V⊗V)[z,z−1]((w))(V\otimes V)[z,z^{-1}]((w)), with 𝒮13(z+w)\mathcal S_{13}(z+w) expanded in nonnegative powers of ww.

A chosen nonidentity exchange need not detect a failure of locality: it may act in a subspace whose products vanish. The next example avoids that ambiguity by producing a nonzero exchange term in the product of two currents.

An odd pole that changes the exchange

Keep the polynomial states V=R[x1,x2,…]V=R[x_1,x_2,\ldots] and Txn=nxn+1Tx_n=nx_{n+1}, but work over R=k[κ,λ]R=k[\kappa,\lambda] with contraction

P(u)=κu−2+λu−1.P(u)=\kappa u^{-2}+\lambda u^{-1}.

Write ∂p=∂/∂xp\partial_p=\partial/\partial x_p, let μ\mu multiply polynomials, and set

Kpq(u)=(−1)q−1P(p+q−2)(u)(p−1)!(q−1)!,C(u)=∑p,q≥1Kpq(u)∂p⊗∂q.K_{pq}(u)=\frac{(-1)^{q-1}P^{(p+q-2)}(u)}{(p-1)!(q-1)!},\qquad C(u)=\sum_{p,q\geq1}K_{pq}(u)\partial_p\otimes\partial_q.

Then define

Y(a,u)b=μ(euT⊗1)eC(u)(a⊗b).Y(a,u)b=\mu(e^{uT}\otimes1)e^{C(u)}(a\otimes b).

On a pair of polynomials the exponential of C(u)C(u) terminates. The translation exponential is interpreted as a formal power series. On J=x1J=x_1 this gives Y(J,u)J=P(u)+(euTJ)JY(J,u)J=P(u)+(e^{uT}J)J. Reversing the separation changes the odd pole’s sign.

Proposition — proved on the polynomial state space

A one-current field algebra with an odd contraction

Use the polynomial states, derivative kernels KpqK_{pq} and finite contraction exponential defined immediately above. The parameters κ\kappa and λ\lambda are independent, and the coefficient ring is k[κ,λ]k[\kappa,\lambda]. All mode derivatives act on polynomial inputs before the resulting Laurent expressions are expanded.

The fields Y(a,u)b=μ(euT⊗1)eC(u)(a⊗b)Y(a,u)b=\mu(e^{uT}\otimes1)e^{C(u)}(a\otimes b) and the exchange 𝒮(z)=exp⁡(∑p,q≥1[Kqp(−z)−Kpq(z)]∂p⊗∂q)\mathcal S(z)=\exp\Bigl(\sum_{p,q\geq1} \bigl[K_{qp}(-z)-K_{pq}(z)\bigr]\, \partial_p\otimes\partial_q\Bigr) form a quantum vertex algebra with rational exchange over k[κ,λ]k[\kappa,\lambda]. On two currents, 𝒮(z)(J⊗J)=J⊗J−2λz−1𝟏⊗𝟏\mathcal S(z)(J\otimes J)=J\otimes J-2\lambda z^{-1}\, \mathbf1\otimes\mathbf1. The exchange is the identity exactly on the locus λ=0\lambda=0, where PP is even.

The proof uses the product rule for the commuting derivatives. Every product of several fields expands from one expression with the exponential of the sum of pair contractions. Reversing two factors replaces C12(u)C_{12}(u) by C21(−u)C_{21}(-u), so their difference supplies the exchange. On two currents that difference is P(−u)−P(u)=−2λ/uP(-u)-P(u)=-2\lambda/u. The exchange disappears precisely when the propagator is even.

There is a further distinction between changing one example and changing an entire category naturally. Charge conjugation sends JJ to −J-J. On J⊗JJ\otimes J, commuting it on the first factor past the exchange gives a nonzero term −4λu−1𝟏⊗𝟏-4\lambda u^{-1}\mathbf1\otimes\mathbf1. A proposed change of tensor that must be natural for this endomorphism cannot simply absorb the odd pole. The corresponding positive changes of marked fields remain available on their separately specified domains. The issue is exactly which morphisms the comparison must preserve.

Several currents and charged states

For a Lie algebra 𝔤\mathfrak g with an invariant symmetric bilinear form BB, its affine current algebra at level KK is generated by currents with singular product

Jx(z)Jy(w)∼KB(x,y)(z−w)2𝟏+J[x,y](w)z−w.J_x(z)J_y(w)\sim\frac{K B(x,y)}{(z-w)^2}\mathbf1+\frac{J_{[x,y]}(w)}{z-w}.

Equivalently, [Jx(m),Jy(n)]=J[x,y](m+n)+mKB(x,y)δm+n,01[J_x(m),J_y(n)]=J_{[x,y]}(m+n)+mK B(x,y)\delta_{m+n,0}1. The simple pole retains the Lie bracket; the double pole retains the invariant form. The vacuum module is generated from a vector killed by the nonnegative modes.

The abelian one-dimensional case recovers Heisenberg. For a nonabelian algebra, discarding the double pole or the trace current can change the dual comparison even if the bracket of the remaining generators is unchanged. This is why the later current–ghost calculations retain the linear, quadratic and scalar relations together.

Let LL be a finite-rank nondegenerate even integral lattice, with bilinear pairing (,)(\ ,\ ), and put 𝔥=L⊗ℂ\mathfrak h=L\otimes\mathbb C. For each α∈L\alpha\in L, the charge space is

Fα=Sym⁡(𝔥⊗t−1ℂ[t−1])eα.F_\alpha=\operatorname{Sym}\bigl(\mathfrak h\otimes t^{-1}\mathbb C[t^{-1}]\bigr)e^\alpha.

For h∈𝔥h\in\mathfrak h and n>0n>0, h(−n)h(-n) multiplies by h⊗t−nh\otimes t^{-n}, while h(n)h(n) is the derivation sending g(−m)g(-m) to n(h,g)δnmn(h,g)\delta_{nm} and killing eαe^\alpha. The zero mode acts by h(0)eα=(h,α)eαh(0)e^\alpha=(h,\alpha)e^\alpha and commutes with all oscillators. Thus FαF_\alpha is a fully specified charged Heisenberg module.

Choose a normalized cocycle ε:L×L→ℂ×\varepsilon:L\times L\to\mathbb C^\times satisfying

ε(0,α)=ε(α,0)=1,ε(α,β)ε(α+β,γ)=ε(β,γ)ε(α,β+γ),ε(α,β)/ε(β,α)=(−1)(α,β).\begin{aligned} \varepsilon(0,\alpha)&=\varepsilon(\alpha,0)=1,\\ \varepsilon(\alpha,\beta)\varepsilon(\alpha+\beta,\gamma) &=\varepsilon(\beta,\gamma)\varepsilon(\alpha,\beta+\gamma),\\ \varepsilon(\alpha,\beta)/\varepsilon(\beta,\alpha)&=(-1)^{(\alpha,\beta)}. \end{aligned}

The lattice vertex algebra is VL=⨁α∈LFαV_L=\bigoplus_{\alpha\in L}F_\alpha with vacuum e0e^0 and the following fields. Let eαeβ=ε(α,β)eα+βe_\alpha e^\beta=\varepsilon(\alpha,\beta)e^{\alpha+\beta}, with eαe_\alpha commuting with the nonzero oscillators, and let zα(0)z^{\alpha(0)} act on FβF_\beta by z(α,β)z^{(\alpha,\beta)}. Then

Y(h(−1)e0,z)=∑n∈ℤh(n)z−n−1,Y(eα,z)=exp⁡(∑n>0α(−n)nzn)exp⁡(−∑n>0α(n)nz−n)eαzα(0).\begin{aligned} Y(h(-1)e^0,z)&=\sum_{n\in\mathbb Z}h(n)z^{-n-1},\\ Y(e^\alpha,z)&= \exp\!\left(\sum_{n>0}\frac{\alpha(-n)}n z^n\right) \exp\!\left(-\sum_{n>0}\frac{\alpha(n)}n z^{-n}\right) e_\alpha z^{\alpha(0)}. \end{aligned}

Translation is determined by Teα=α(−1)eαTe^\alpha=\alpha(-1)e^\alpha and [T,h(−n)]=nh(−n−1)[T,h(-n)]=n h(-n-1). For a state h1(−n1)⋯hr(−nr)eαh_1(-n_1)\cdots h_r(-n_r)e^\alpha, its field is the right-nested normal product of ∂zni−1Y(hi(−1)e0,z)/(ni−1)!\partial_z^{n_i-1}Y(h_i(-1)e^0,z)/(n_i-1)! with Y(eα,z)Y(e^\alpha,z). These formulas specify every field. The annihilation exponential is finite on each polynomial input, while the creation exponential is a formal power series. In particular,

eα(z)eβ(w)=ε(α,β)(z−w)(α,β)(eα+β(w)+oscillator descendants).e^\alpha(z)e^\beta(w)=\varepsilon(\alpha,\beta)(z-w)^{(\alpha,\beta)}\bigl(e^{\alpha+\beta}(w)+\text{oscillator descendants}\bigr).

The oscillator descendants in this last expression are exactly the terms of the two displayed exponentials and their derivatives. Even integrality and the cocycle supply the signs needed for locality. Allowing fractional pairings requires a choice of branches and a different field domain. The charged comparisons below use the nondegenerate case.

Monodromy is the automorphism obtained by continuing a local solution around a closed path. For a scalar factor zaz^a, one positive circuit multiplies it by e2πiae^{2\pi ia}. A positive half circuit and its clockwise inverse are different paths. Two positive half circuits need not cancel. In the line comparisons below, a gauge between two differential equations, a horizontal section of either equation, and an evaluated distribution can consequently have different continuation properties.

The free paired systems provide another useful control. Even fields βi,γj\beta_i,\gamma^j have contraction βi(z)γj(w)∼δij/(z−w)\beta_i(z)\gamma^j(w)\sim\delta_i^j/(z-w); their odd counterparts use the parity sign when factors are exchanged. These systems make the dependence on coefficients, derivatives and signs explicit before an interacting comparison is attempted.

Why complexes enter the reconstruction

An operator identity may hold only after adding a correction whose differential is the error. The correction is part of the structure: further compositions must retain it. Complexes organize these equations.

A graded vector space is a direct sum V=⨁iViV=\bigoplus_iV^i with specified degrees. A cochain complex is such a space with maps d:Vi→Vi+1d:V^i\to V^{i+1} satisfying d2=0d^2=0. Its cohomology is Hi(V)=ker⁡(d:Vi→Vi+1)/im⁡(d:Vi−1→Vi)H^i(V)=\ker(d:V^i\to V^{i+1})/\operatorname{im}(d:V^{i-1}\to V^i). Thus a closed element is zero in cohomology precisely when it has a primitive.

The abbreviation dg means differential graded. A differential graded algebra is a cochain complex with associative multiplication of degree zero, a unit, and d(ab)=d(a)b+(−1)|a|ad(b)d(ab)=d(a)b+(-1)^{|a|}a\,d(b). A homotopy between cochain maps f,gf,g is a map hh of degree −1-1 satisfying f−g=dh+hdf-g=dh+hd. A quasi-isomorphism is a cochain map inducing isomorphisms on every cohomology group.

Formality of a dg algebra is a further property: an equivalence of dg algebras, possibly through a chain of quasi-isomorphisms, with its cohomology algebra equipped with zero differential. It differs from interpreting a series formally.

Odd variables make a small calculation decisive. On k[x]⊗Λ(c−1,c0)k[x]\otimes\Lambda(c_{-1},c_0), let Q=∂xc−1+xc0Q=\partial_xc_{-1}+xc_0, with the ghosts acting by exterior multiplication. The square is

Q2=c−1c0[∂x,x]=c−1c0.Q^2=c_{-1}c_0[\partial_x,x]=c_{-1}c_0.

The two individual squares vanish, but their mixed terms retain the current commutator. This QQ alone is not a differential. A consistent coupled construction must account for its square, for the differential of its coefficients, and for any specified curvature. Checking only one of those terms changes the equation.

The BRST construction adds odd variables for infinitesimal symmetries and a differential encoding both their action and their relations. For a Lie algebra action ρ\rho with structure constants fbcaf^a_{bc}, its Chevalley differential contains caρa−12fbcacbcc∂cac^a\rho_a-\tfrac12 f^a_{bc}c^bc^c\partial_{c^a}. Its square vanishes when the action relations and Jacobi identity hold. In curved comparisons the extra square and the specified curvature must instead satisfy their stated compatibility equation.

The examples have now isolated three requirements. A reconstruction must retain the poles and all states on which they act. It must distinguish the local identity from scalar evaluation. It must also retain the corrections to composition, on the same coefficient and support domain as the operations themselves. The geometric definitions implement these requirements at every number of insertions.

3Definitions and geometry

Coefficients that can meet and separate

The examples use points in a curve and operators on a state space. To compare them geometrically, we need to say where the coefficients live and what happens when points coincide. A carrier is this specified geometric and categorical domain: for example, complexes of differential modules on all powers of a curve, with specified restriction maps. A construction is native when it uses that domain’s own objects, maps and tensor product. An algebra of matrices obtained after forgetting positions may provide a useful comparison, but its endomorphisms need not be native operations.

For a space XX and a finite label set II, the configuration space of distinct labelled points is the open subset of XIX^I on which xi≠xjx_i\ne x_j for i≠ji\ne j. We also use the ambient space XIX^I to retain coincidences. A collision stratum specifies which coordinates are equal. The pair diagonal is Δij={xi=xj}\Delta_{ij}=\{x_i=x_j\}. A spectator is an insertion retained while an operation is performed on other labels; its position, coefficient and intervening place in an order remain part of the operation’s input.

On three positions, the collision x1=x3x_1=x_3 leaves x2x_2 as a spectator. The product E12E21E12=E12E_{12}E_{21}E_{12}=E_{12} of elementary matrices, compared with E122=0E_{12}^2=0, shows why the middle operation cannot be deleted. A construction that remembers only the set of occupied points loses this information.

A right differential-module on a smooth space YY is a sheaf with a right action of the algebra 𝒟Y\mathcal D_Y of differential operators, with quasi-coherent underlying 𝒪Y\mathcal O_Y-module in the coefficient category used here. In one coordinate, ∂zf−f∂z=f′\partial_z f-f\partial_z=f'. The action includes both multiplication by functions and differentiation, and agrees under coordinate changes.

The operator algebra is already noncommutative before any quantization of the fields: differentiation does not commute with multiplication by the coordinate. Differential modules consequently retain differentiation transverse to a collision, as well as values along it.

The derived category identifies quasi-isomorphic complexes; here an enhancement also retains their mapping complexes and coherent homotopies. A mapping space records maps, homotopies between maps, and higher homotopies. Its set of connected components alone is insufficient for specifying a coherently associative action. The heart for the usual cohomological grading consists of objects whose cohomology is concentrated in degree zero.

The derived tensor product M⊗R𝕃NM\otimes_R^{\mathbb L}N is computed by replacing a factor with a resolution whose tensor product preserves quasi-isomorphisms. It retains the extra cohomology that ordinary tensoring can lose. For instance, over R=k[u]R=k[u], the resolution [R→uR][R\xrightarrow{u}R] of k=R/(u)k=R/(u) gives k⊗R𝕃k=[k→0k]k\otimes_R^{\mathbb L}k=[k\xrightarrow{0}k], with nonzero terms in degrees −1-1 and 00.

For a smooth map or embedding f:Z→Yf:Z\to Y, write f!f^! for extraordinary inverse image and f+f_+ for differential-module direct image. With right modules, the conventions are

f+M=Rf*𝒪(M⊗𝒟Z𝕃𝒟Z→Y),f!N=(f−1N⊗f−1𝒟Y𝕃𝒟Y←Z)[dim⁡Z−dim⁡Y].f_+M=Rf_*^{\mathcal O}(M\otimes_{\mathcal D_Z}^{\mathbb L}\mathcal D_{Z\to Y}),\qquad f^!N=(f^{-1}N\otimes_{f^{-1}\mathcal D_Y}^{\mathbb L}\mathcal D_{Y\leftarrow Z})[\dim Z-\dim Y].

Here 𝒟Z→Y=𝒪Z⊗f−1𝒪Yf−1𝒟Y\mathcal D_{Z\to Y}=\mathcal O_Z\otimes_{f^{-1}\mathcal O_Y}f^{-1}\mathcal D_Y, and 𝒟Y←Z\mathcal D_{Y\leftarrow Z} converts the left and right actions using the canonical lines of top forms. The symbol Rf*𝒪Rf_*^{\mathcal O} denotes derived sheaf direct image. These formulas fix the dimension shifts. The dualizing coefficient is JY=ωY[dim⁡Y]J_Y=\omega_Y[\dim Y], whose exceptional fibre at a smooth point is kk in degree zero. For an open immersion jj, j!j^! is restriction and we write j*j_* for j+j_+. For a closed immersion ii we similarly write i*i_*.

The normal derivatives along u=0u=0 are derivatives in the coordinate transverse to that locus. A differential module supported there contains the corresponding derivatives of the delta distribution, not merely a function on the locus. The principal parts at u=0u=0 are polar expressions modulo regular expressions, such as k[u,u−1]/k[u]k[u,u^{-1}]/k[u]. They include every pole order admitted by the coefficient domain.

For a closed subset Z⊂YZ\subset Y, with open complement j:U↪Yj:U\hookrightarrow Y, local cohomology is the derived object of sections supported on ZZ:

RΓZ(M)=fib⁡(M→j*j!M).R\Gamma_Z(M)=\operatorname{fib}(M\longrightarrow j_*j^!M).

For a closed embedding in the differential-module category it is i*i!Mi_*i^!M. The fibre is a complex, so it can retain a supported class in a degree where an ordinary kernel vanishes.

These distinctions fix the meaning of a collision coefficient. Localization permits poles; a supported direct image retains their normal derivatives; extraordinary restriction and local cohomology retain the derived terms. Replacing all three with evaluation at u=0u=0 would change the construction.

Words, cuts and the empty unit

The ordered word carrier is

𝒲X=D(k)×lim←OrdSurj⁡+DMod⁡(Xn).\mathcal W_X=D(k)\times\underset{\longleftarrow}{\lim}_{\operatorname{OrdSurj}_+}\operatorname{DMod}(X^n).

The index category has nonempty finite ordered sets and monotone surjections. A surjection α:[n]↠[m]\alpha:[n]\twoheadrightarrow[m] gives the diagonal dα(x)i=xα(i)d_\alpha(x)_i=x_{\alpha(i)}; the transition is dα!d_\alpha^!. Objects include the resulting identifications and their coherences. The separate factor D(k)D(k) supplies the empty coefficient. At the level of points, words are identified only by inserting or deleting adjacent equal entries.

Thus abab, abaaba and abababab are different reduced words when a≠ba\ne b, even though they have the same occupied positions. This is the carrier needed for the outer collision in the matrix calculation.

For 1≤p<n1\le p<n, let Up⊂XnU_p\subset X^n be the open set where xi≠xjx_i\ne x_j for every i≤p<ji\le p<j, with inclusion jpj_p. The cut product is

(F⋆cutG)n=⨁p=0njp,*(Fp⊠Gn−p)|Up.(F\star_{\mathrm{cut}}G)_n=\bigoplus_{p=0}^n j_{p,*}(F_p\boxtimes G_{n-p})|_{U_p}.

Here ⊠\boxtimes is the external product on independent position spaces. Empty blocks mean scalar tensoring on the whole space. The unit KK is kk at the empty word and zero elsewhere. The sum uses consecutive cuts. Its iterates use consecutive partitions with every pair of different blocks disjoint.

Associativity follows because either bracketing of several factors gives that same expression over consecutive partitions. Collision compatibility uses open base change. A cut inside a fibre of a monotone collapse has empty inverse image; a cut between fibres descends to a cut in the shorter word. No symmetry of this tensor is assumed.

The locus at which every consecutive cut is crossed by an equality is

Z1=X,Zn=⋂p=1n−1⋃i≤p<jΔij.Z_1=X,\qquad Z_n=\bigcap_{p=1}^{n-1}\ \bigcup_{i\le p<j}\Delta_{ij}.

In particular,

Z2=Δ12,Z3=Δ13,Z4=Δ14∪(Δ13∩Δ24).Z_2=\Delta_{12},\qquad Z_3=\Delta_{13},\qquad Z_4=\Delta_{14}\cup(\Delta_{13}\cap\Delta_{24}).

The three-position locus includes (x,y,x)(x,y,x) with x≠yx\ne y. The four-position formula contains a union of two different possibilities. Replacing it with the small diagonal, or with the intersection of every pair diagonal, changes the support of the algebra.

A coalgebra for a specified tensor product has a coassociative coproduct C→C⋆CC\to C\star C and a counit to the tensor unit. A coaugmentation is a compatible map from that unit to CC. In the enhanced category the axioms include coherent homotopies.

Factorization means that coefficients over separated groups of positions are identified with the external products of their coefficients. A factorization coalgebra for the cut product is a coaugmented coalgebra for which each component

Cn|Up→(Cp⊠Cn−p)|UpC_n|_{U_p}\longrightarrow(C_p\boxtimes C_{n-p})|_{U_p}

is an equivalence, coherently under further cuts. It is also called strong. This condition is imposed on each specified separating map; a statement about the sum of several components can be different.

The second geometric carrier

The ordered collision atlas has a chart XIX^I for each total order on a finite set II. Two charts are glued on the open set where every pair on which their orders disagree has distinct coordinates. Over a configuration with equality blocks BB, the resulting scheme ℛI\mathscr R_I has ∏B|B|!\prod_B|B|! points. Each point retains a total order within every collision block.

Orders are forgotten for distinct points and retained for coincident ones. For two labels the two charts agree off the diagonal but have separate diagonal branches. This is a different construction from words modulo adjacent repetitions.

On these schemes, coefficients have coherent extraordinary-pullback identifications along ordered collision maps. Their convolution sums over all ordered decompositions I=A⊔BI=A\sqcup B into subsets, rather than only initial and final intervals. If qA,B:ℛI→ℛA×ℛBq_{A,B}:\mathscr R_I\to\mathscr R_A\times\mathscr R_B forgets the cross order and jA,Bj_{A,B} includes the locus separating the two blocks, the summand is

jA,B,*jA,B!qA,B!(FA⊠GB).j_{A,B,*}j_{A,B}^!q_{A,B}^!(F_A\boxtimes G_B).

The resulting convolution is symmetric monoidal and again has empty unit KK. Its componentwise factorization condition asks for an equivalence for every ordered decomposition. Forgetting to consecutive cuts supplies a comparison with the word construction; it does not identify the two carriers.

At two distinct positions, two componentwise equivalences have joint map (1,R):V→V⊕V(1,R):V\to V\oplus V. Its cofiber is VV, by (x,y)↦y−Rx(x,y)\mapsto y-Rx. In contrast, the bar of an algebra supported on the small diagonal has two singleton words and coproduct projections V⊕V→VV\oplus V\to V. Neither projection is an equivalence when V≠0V\ne0, although their joint map is. This calculation separates componentwise factorization from joint word factorization. Both are useful conditions, on different objects.

From products to a coalgebra, and back

The suspension of a cochain complex here is sV=V[1]sV=V[1], so ss has degree −1-1. An A-infinity algebra has operations mnm_n of degree 2−n2-n whose identities express associativity with all coherent corrections. Equivalently, the corresponding degree-one coderivation on the tensor coalgebra of sVsV squares to zero. The first identity is m12=0m_1^2=0; the next says that m1m_1 is compatible with m2m_2; the next allows the associator of m2m_2 to be the differential of m3m_3.

For an augmented algebra A→KA\to K with positive ideal A¯\overline A (zero at the empty configuration), the bar coalgebra is

BA=K⊕⨁r≥1(sA¯)⋆r.BA=K\oplus\bigoplus_{r\ge1}(s\overline A)^{\star r}.

Its coproduct cuts a tensor word into two words. On a strict dg algebra its differential is the coderivation determined by

b1(sa)=−s(da),b2(sa⊗sb)=(−1)|a|s(ab).b_1(sa)=-s(da),\qquad b_2(sa\otimes sb)=(-1)^{|a|}s(ab).

For a coaugmented coalgebra C=K⊕C¯C=K\oplus\overline C, its cobar ΩC\Omega C is the tensor algebra on tC¯=C¯[−1]t\overline C=\overline C[-1], with differential determined by

d(tc)=−t(dc)+∑(−1)|c′|+1(tc′)(tc″),Δ¯c=∑c′⊗c″.d(tc)=-t(dc)+\sum(-1)^{|c'|+1}(tc')(tc''),\qquad \overline\Delta c=\sum c'\otimes c''.

The bar–cobar comparison consists of the natural maps ΩBA→A\Omega BA\to A and C→BΩCC\to B\Omega C. Coherent versions retain the higher operations.

A product of rr positive systems vanishes on fewer than rr labels. Consequently each configuration sees only finitely many normalized word lengths. The equivalence proved below uses this bound even for unbounded coefficient complexes. It is an associative construction. The Lie–commutative duality of Francis and Gaitsgory has different algebraic operations and does not supply this associative comparison.

An associative chiral algebra now combines the associative product with the separation condition. The selected convolution is part of its definition. A left differential module can be converted to a right one by tensoring with ωX\omega_X; a horizontal map commutes with the differential-operator actions. These conventions interpret the vacuum clause in the complete definition.

Definition

An associative algebra whose bar separates configurations

Choose either the word cut convolution or the ordered collision convolution defined above. The empty unit is KK. “Positive” means zero empty coefficient. The bar is the finite-at-each-configuration construction above; its factorization condition uses the separating maps of the chosen convolution.

For either specified convolution, an associative chiral algebra is an augmented associative algebra AA whose augmentation ideal is positive and whose bar BABA is factorizing.

A vacuum marking consists of a left differential module GG, a horizontal map 𝒪X→G\mathcal O_X\to G, and an identification A{1}≅ωX⊗𝒪XGA_{\{1\}}\cong\omega_X\otimes_{\mathcal O_X}G. A vacuum framing also specifies a comparison with ordered simultaneous products on GG, preserving substitutions, translation and that vacuum.

The empty augmentation and the nonempty vacuum are therefore specified separately. The definition does not require a scalar character on every field state. On words, factorization of BABA is equivalent to support of A¯n\overline A_n on ZnZ_n. On the atlas, the binary calculation above shows why the same componentwise condition need not imply small-diagonal support.

What the second algebra means

The bar produces a coalgebra. Producing a second algebra requires a duality on coefficients and a decision about its tensor. In this account Koszul duality denotes the specified passage between algebraic structures through their bar construction and the applicable duality; the domain and recipient must accompany the term. A resolution ΩBA≃A\Omega BA\simeq A alone has not identified a second algebra of fields.

A completion is taken with respect to a stated filtration or system of quotients, such as M̂=lim←mM/FmM\widehat M=\underset{\longleftarrow}{\lim}_m M/F^mM. A formal parameter ℏ\hbar specifies the quotients by ℏm\hbar^m. For a topologically free field module the target can be lim←m(V/ℏmV)((z))\underset{\longleftarrow}{\lim}_m(V/\hbar^mV)((z)): the allowed pole bound is finite at each precision, but need not be uniform in mm.

A continuous dual consists of linear maps continuous for the stated topology on the source and target. It depends on those topologies. A dual formed degree by degree under finite-dimensionality hypotheses, a continuous dual of a completed space, and a pro-object of finite duals are distinct constructions unless a comparison is supplied.

For a smooth affine chart UU of dimension dd, put D=Γ(U,𝒟U)D=\Gamma(U,\mathcal D_U). A perfect right DD-complex is a retract of a finite complex of finite-rank free modules. Its finite-cell dual is

P†=(RHom⁡D(P,D))t[d],t(f)=f,t(∂i)=−∂i,t(PQ)=t(Q)t(P).P^\dagger=(R\operatorname{Hom}_D(P,D))^t[d],\qquad t(f)=f,\quad t(\partial_i)=-\partial_i,\quad t(PQ)=t(Q)t(P).

The canonical line makes this independent of a coordinate volume. On holonomic differential modules, Verdier duality is the functor given by this derived-Hom formula, with the canonical-line conversion and dimension shift displayed above. It exchanges direct-image extension with its dual extension. The finite-cell operation extends the differential-module duality to a larger recipient: for M=colim⁡αPαM=\operatorname{colim}_\alpha P_\alpha, retain the entire pro-diagram M♯={Pα†}αM^\sharp=\{P_\alpha^\dagger\}_\alpha. A pro-diagram includes all stages and transition maps; it is not its ordinary inverse limit.

For example, D[u−1]D[u^{-1}] is the colimit of repeated left multiplication by uu on DD. Its dual is the inverse diagram with the same transitions on D[1]D[1]. No transition becomes zero, so the pro-object is nonzero; its underived inverse limit is zero because ⋂nunD=0\bigcap_nu^nD=0. This example prevents replacing the recipient silently by ordinary differential modules.

The full coefficient construction transports the geometric functors and the tensor along ♯\sharp. It supplies an algebra on the transported tensor. An essential image is the class of objects isomorphic to outputs of a specified functor. The further question is whether that algebra lies in the essential image of a field construction, and whether its transported tensor agrees with the physical tensor under a proved comparison.

A commutative vertex algebra is a commutative differential algebra with derivation TT and fields Y(a,z)b=(ezTa)bY(a,z)b=(e^{zT}a)b, with graded signs when states are odd. Its products on itself have no singular part. Its modules can nevertheless have nonzero singular modes, so a curvature density can act nontrivially on a module.

The current example has another dual description. The odd differential polynomial algebra Λ[c,Tc,T2c,…]\Lambda[c,Tc,T^2c,\ldots] retains the Heisenberg level through the degree-two density w=κcTc/2w=\kappa cTc/2. For its curved modules the square is Q2=−w(0)Q^2=-w_{(0)}. A density means a state modulo total derivatives, because (Ta)(0)=0(Ta)_{(0)}=0 on every module.

A Maurer–Cartan equation in a dg Lie algebra is dq+12[q,q]=0dq+\tfrac12[q,q]=0 for a degree-one element qq. With a specified central curvature ww it becomes dq+12[q,q]+w=0dq+\tfrac12[q,q]+w=0. For the field coupling it is an equation modulo total translation derivatives.

Definition

A curved commutative algebra of fields

Here RR is a commutative characteristic-zero coefficient algebra, TT is translation, and a(n)a_{(n)} is the nnth mode of the state aa. The grading determines all super signs. The condition dw∈TAdw\in TA says that the curvature is closed modulo total derivatives.

A curved commutative vertex algebra over RR is a triple (A,d,w)(A,d,w). Here (A,d)(A,d) is a commutative differential graded vertex superalgebra over RR, and w∈A2w\in A^2 is a state with dw∈TAdw\in TA. It is an algebra, not a coalgebra, and its product is the commutative one.

A morphism (A,d,w)→(A′,d′,w′)(A,d,w)\to(A',d',w') is a morphism ff of differential graded vertex algebras with f(w)−w′∈TA′f(w)-w'\in TA'. A curved vertex module of (A,d,w)(A,d,w) is a graded module FF of the vertex algebra AA with an operator QQ of degree one. It satisfies [Q,a(n)]=(da)(n),Q2=−w(0)[Q,a_{(n)}]=(da)_{(n)},\qquad Q^2=-w_{(0)} for every state aa and every integer nn.

Definition

The current–ghost coupling as a twisting state

Use the curved commutative vertex algebra (A,d,w)(A,d,w) just defined and a vertex algebra VV concentrated in degree zero. Tensor products are over RR. In the displayed equation TT is the total translation of the two factors; q(0)qq_{(0)}q is the zero-mode product.

Let VV be a vertex algebra over RR in degree zero, and let (A,d,w)(A,d,w) be a curved commutative vertex algebra over RR. A twisting state is a state qq of degree one in V⊗RAV\otimes_RA with dq+12q(0)q+w∈T(V⊗RA).\begin{equation} dq+\tfrac12\,q_{(0)}q+w\in T(V\otimes_RA). \end{equation}

This quadratic field construction recovers the current relations by a universal coupling. It does not, by itself, identify its module category with the bar construction’s module category. The full coefficient dual, this curved field dual, and the internal dual for the product along a line have different definitions. Their comparison is part of the problem.

Symmetries with a separation parameter

A bialgebra is an algebra HH and a coalgebra (H,Δ,ε)(H,\Delta,\varepsilon) for which Δ\Delta and ε\varepsilon preserve multiplication and unit. A Hopf algebra also has an antipode 𝗌\mathsf s satisfying μ(𝗌⊗1)Δ=μ(1⊗𝗌)Δ=1ε\mu(\mathsf s\otimes1)\Delta=\mu(1\otimes\mathsf s)\Delta=1\varepsilon. A right comodule is a module MM with a counital, coassociative map δ:M→M⊗H\delta:M\to M\otimes H. We write Δa=∑a1⊗a2\Delta a=\sum a_1\otimes a_2 and δ(m)=∑m(0)⊗m(1)\delta(m)=\sum m_{(0)}\otimes m_{(1)}.

A quantum group supplies algebraic symmetry together with a compatible rule for combining and exchanging representations. The spectral construction here starts from a flat Hopf algebra and a derivation and coderivation TT with εT=0\varepsilon T=0. The separation of two positions is the parameter zz.

A coquasitriangular form describes exchange by a bilinear form on a Hopf algebra, so that its values on the tails of two coactions interchange the comodule factors. A spectral form allows this bilinear form to depend rationally on separation, with prescribed translation and reversal identities. The complete axioms below include both multiplicativity rules, their order convention, and the compatibility with the Hopf product. Merely choosing a rational function does not supply these axioms.

Definition

A unitary spectral form on a Hopf algebra

Let HH be a flat Hopf algebra over RR with bijective antipode and a derivation and coderivation TT satisfying εT=0\varepsilon T=0. Put a(z)=ezTaa(z)=e^{zT}a. The subscripts a1,a2a_1,a_2 denote coproduct components with the finite sum understood. All six identities are required.

A unitary spectral coquasitriangular form on HH is an RR-bilinear map ρz:H⊗H→R[z,z−1]\rho_z\colon H\otimes H\to R[z,z^{-1}] with the following properties: ρz(1,a)=ε(a)=ρz(a,1),ρz(ab,c)=ρz(a,c1)ρz(b,c2),ρz(a,bc)=ρz(a1,c)ρz(a2,b),ρz(a1,b1)a2(z)b2=b1a1(z)ρz(a2,b2),ρz(Ta,b)=∂zρz(a,b)=−ρz(a,Tb),ρz(a1,b1)ρ−z(b2,a2)=ε(a)ε(b).\begin{align} \rho_z(1,a)&=\varepsilon(a)=\rho_z(a,1), \\ \rho_z(ab,c)&=\rho_z(a,c_1)\rho_z(b,c_2), \\ \rho_z(a,bc)&=\rho_z(a_1,c)\rho_z(a_2,b), \\ \rho_z(a_1,b_1)a_2(z)b_2 &=b_1a_1(z)\rho_z(a_2,b_2), \\ \rho_z(Ta,b)&=\partial_z\rho_z(a,b)=-\rho_z(a,Tb), \\ \rho_z(a_1,b_1)\rho_{-z}(b_2,a_2) &=\varepsilon(a)\varepsilon(b). \end{align} The fourth displayed identity is an identity in H[[z]][z−1]H[[z]][z^{-1}]. The order of the two factors in the third displayed identity is part of the convention.

The word “unitary” here means that reversing an exchange gives its inverse. It does not assert positivity of a Hilbert-space inner product. In this setting a level, generalizing the scalar parameter in the first example, is a Hopf automorphism η\eta commuting with TT and preserving ρz\rho_z. Levels compose as automorphisms and need not commute.

Definition

Levels as symmetries of the Hopf and spectral data

The Hopf algebra HH, translation TT and form ρz\rho_z are fixed as above. The word level in this general definition means an automorphism preserving these data. This includes families whose scalar current level is encoded by the chosen automorphism.

A level is a Hopf automorphism η\eta of HH such that ηT=Tη\eta T=T\eta and ρz(ηa,ηb)=ρz(a,b)\rho_z(\eta a,\eta b)=\rho_z(a,b). Levels form a group under composition, with η1η2=η1∘η2\eta_1\eta_2=\eta_1\circ\eta_2.

Definition

A spectral presentation of chiral symmetry

Here kk has characteristic zero, RR is a commutative kk-algebra, and the curve is the affine line with coordinate zz. The spectral-form axioms and level group have been displayed in full above. All Hopf algebras in this definition are in cohomological degree zero.

A spectral chiral quantum group over RR consists of the following data.

  1. A flat Hopf algebra HH over RR in degree zero, with bijective antipode 𝗌\mathsf s. It carries an RR-linear derivation and coderivation TT with εT=0\varepsilon T=0.

  2. A unitary spectral coquasitriangular form ρz:H⊗H→R[z,z−1]\rho_z\colon H\otimes H\to R[z,z^{-1}] on HH (with the complete spectral-form axioms above).

  3. A group Λ\Lambda of levels of (H,T,ρz)(H,T,\rho_z) (with the level convention above).

A morphism (H,T,ρz,Λ)→(H′,T′,ρz′,Λ′)(H,T,\rho_z,\Lambda)\to(H',T',\rho'_z,\Lambda') is a map of Hopf algebras f:H→H′f\colon H\to H' with fT=T′ffT=T'f and ρz′(fa,fb)=ρz(a,b)\rho'_z(fa,fb)=\rho_z(a,b), together with a homomorphism Λ→Λ′\Lambda\to\Lambda', η↦η′\eta\mapsto\eta', such that fη=η′ff\eta=\eta'f.

An H-covariant field algebra is a quantum vertex algebra VV with a right coaction δ(v)=∑v(0)⊗v(1)\delta(v)=\sum v_{(0)}\otimes v_{(1)} that preserves the vacuum and satisfies

δTV=(TV⊗1+1⊗T)δ,δ(Y(a,z)b)=Y(a(0),z)b(0)⊗b(1)a(1)(z),𝒮(z)(a⊗b)=a(0)⊗b(0)ρz(a(1),b(1)).\begin{aligned} \delta T_V&=(T_V\otimes1+1\otimes T)\delta,\\ \delta(Y(a,z)b)&=Y(a_{(0)},z)b_{(0)}\otimes b_{(1)}a_{(1)}(z),\\ \mathcal S(z)(a\otimes b)&=a_{(0)}\otimes b_{(0)}\rho_z(a_{(1)},b_{(1)}). \end{aligned}

All finite ordered products on a fixed state must expand common rational germs with finite pole order at each collision. Morphisms preserve fields, vacuum, translation and coaction. The crossed field product V1⊠ρV2V_1\boxtimes_\rho V_2 has underlying module V1⊗V2V_1\otimes V_2 and operations

Y12(a⊗b,z)(c⊗d)=Y1(a,z)c(0)⊗Y2(b(0),z)dρ−z(c(1),b(1)),δ12(a⊗b)=a(0)⊗b(0)⊗b(1)a(1).\begin{aligned} Y_{12}(a\otimes b,z)(c\otimes d) &=Y_1(a,z)c_{(0)}\otimes Y_2(b_{(0)},z)d\, \rho_{-z}(c_{(1)},b_{(1)}),\\ \delta_{12}(a\otimes b)&=a_{(0)}\otimes b_{(0)}\otimes b_{(1)}a_{(1)}. \end{aligned}

Its vacuum is 𝟏⊗𝟏\mathbf1\otimes\mathbf1, translation is T1⊗1+1⊗T2T_1\otimes1+1\otimes T_2, and exchange is obtained from this coaction by the preceding formula. In particular the order of the two coaction tails is reversed. This is a field product on the ordinary tensor module, distinct from an external product on separate position spaces.

The state space at level η\eta is HH with fields constructed from the spectral data. The level-changing map Dη1,η2=(η2⊗1)ΔD_{\eta_1,\eta_2}=(\eta_2\otimes1)\Delta has recipient Vη1⊠ρVη2V_{\eta_1}\boxtimes_\rho V_{\eta_2}. It combines states at one position. The cut coproduct instead separates groups of positions.

A monoidal category has a tensor, a unit and coherent associativity and unit isomorphisms. A monoidal functor preserves them with coherent comparison maps. Its tensorator is the specified comparison between F(M)⊗F(N)F(M)\otimes F(N) and F(M⊗N)F(M\otimes N); for a strong monoidal functor it is an isomorphism. Naturality requires this comparison to commute with every admitted morphism, not just with the action on a chosen generator.

Over a field kk, a fibre functor on a kk-linear abelian monoidal category 𝒞\mathcal C is an exact faithful kk-linear strong monoidal functor F:𝒞→Vect⁡kfdF:\mathcal C\to\operatorname{Vect}^{\mathrm{fd}}_k, where the recipient consists of finite-dimensional vector spaces. Exactness preserves short exact sequences, and faithfulness means that the map on each space of morphisms is injective. The tensor and unit comparisons are isomorphisms; preservation of a symmetry is an additional requirement. Forgetting the action on a finite-dimensional group representation is an example.

The dimension function of a fibre functor FF is dF(X)=dim⁡kF(X)d_F(X)=\dim_kF(X). It is additive on short exact sequences and multiplicative on tensor products, with dF(𝟏)=1d_F(\mathbf1)=1. If XX has a dual, then dF(X∨)=dF(X)d_F(X^\vee)=d_F(X), because a strong monoidal functor preserves the evaluation and coevaluation that exhibit the dual. The ordinary dimension of a group representation is the example supplied by the forgetful functor.

The categorical definition retains translation and exchange while treating a compatible Hopf presentation as a choice. Such a presentation identifies the category with finite projective comodules of a flat Hopf algebra with bijective antipode, and requires every flat comodule to be a union of such finite subcomodules. A formal family means a compatible system modulo znz^n; a pole is allowed to have finite order on each finite subobject. With these conventions the definition is as follows.

Definition

The category with translation and spectral exchange

A presentation is a monoidal equivalence with finite projective comodules of a flat Hopf algebra with bijective antipode, with the union condition for flat comodules stated above. Formal families and their finite-pole morphisms are interpreted coefficientwise. The translation acts on objects and morphisms, so both sides of each identity have the stated positioned source and target.

An intrinsic chiral quantum group over RR is an RR-linear monoidal category 𝒞\mathcal C with left and right duals and two further structures. One condition is imposed.

  1. A translation: a family of monoidal autoequivalences M↦M(z)M\mapsto M(z) of 𝒞\mathcal C, formal in zz, with M(0)=MM(0)=M and M(z)(w)=M(z+w)M(z)(w)=M(z+w).

  2. A symmetry: morphisms σM,N(z):M(z)⊗N→N⊗M(z)\sigma_{M,N}(z)\colon M(z)\otimes N\to N\otimes M(z) with poles at z=0z=0, natural in M,NM,N. Write τu\tau_u for translation by uu, on objects and morphisms. The maps with the unit object are the canonical identifications.

    The two hexagons are σM⊗N,P(z)=(σM,P(z)⊗1N(z))(1M(z)⊗σN,P(z)),σM,N⊗P(z)=(1N⊗σM,P(z))(σM,N(z)⊗1P).\begin{align*} \sigma_{M\otimes N,P}(z) &=(\sigma_{M,P}(z)\otimes1_{N(z)}) (1_{M(z)}\otimes\sigma_{N,P}(z)),\\ \sigma_{M,N\otimes P}(z) &=(1_N\otimes\sigma_{M,P}(z)) (\sigma_{M,N}(z)\otimes1_P). \end{align*} Unitarity means τz(σN,M(−z))σM,N(z)=1M(z)⊗N.\tau_z\bigl(\sigma_{N,M}(-z)\bigr)\sigma_{M,N}(z) =1_{M(z)\otimes N}. The translation identity is σM(u),N(z)=σM,N(z+u)=τu(σM,N(−u)(z)).\begin{equation} \sigma_{M(u),N}(z)=\sigma_{M,N}(z+u) =\tau_u\bigl(\sigma_{M,N(-u)}(z)\bigr). \end{equation} Monoidal constraints are understood in these identities. In the displayed translation identity, expand at u=0u=0 after localizing in zz. Identities in several separations are compared before choosing their Laurent expansions.

  3. The condition: there is a presentation ω\omega with a derivation and coderivation TT of HωH_\omega, εT=0\varepsilon T=0. It carries the translation to M↦M(z)M\mapsto M(z) and σ\sigma to a spectral comodule symmetry for (Hω,T)(H_\omega,T).

A level is a monoidal autoequivalence of 𝒞\mathcal C that commutes with the translation and preserves σ\sigma. Levels are composed as functors, and their isomorphism classes form a group Λ(𝒞)\Lambda(\mathcal C).

Its exchange has source M(z)⊗NM(z)\otimes N, so an ordinary braiding M⊗N→N⊗MM\otimes N\to N\otimes M cannot replace it. A geometric version must additionally construct the position spaces, collision maps and separation equivalences of its categories. The categorical spectral definition does not make that geometric extension automatic.

Products along a line and their centres

At fixed holomorphic position, two insertions can still be ordered along a transverse real line. On coefficient systems the corresponding tensor is F⊗!G=Δ!(F⊠G)F\otimes^!G=\Delta^!(F\boxtimes G), with dualizing unit JJ. It combines coefficients at the same positions. The convolution ⋆\star combines coefficients of separate labelled blocks and has empty unit KK.

The forward interchange

(F⋆G)⊗!(H⋆L)→(F⊗!H)⋆(G⊗!L)(F\star G)\otimes^!(H\star L)\longrightarrow(F\otimes^!H)\star(G\otimes^!L)

projects onto summands with matching decompositions. It makes coaugmented convolution coalgebras a symmetric monoidal category for ⊗!\otimes^!, with unit JJ. The reverse inclusion exists in positive arities, but their composite on the larger sum is a projection, not the identity.

A transverse monoid is the associative algebra object for this second tensor. Its vacuum is a map from JJ, hence a compatible vacuum at every configuration. The full definition also fixes its actions.

Definition

The product at one holomorphic position

Let Coalg\mathrm{Coalg} denote coaugmented, counital convolution coalgebras with empty coefficient kk. Their diagonal tensor is ⊗!\otimes^!, their unit is the dualizing coalgebra JJ, and the forward interchange is the common-decomposition projection described above. This category includes the coherent maps used in the definition.

A transverse monoid is an associative algebra object of the symmetric monoidal category (Coalg⁡,⊗!,J)(\operatorname{Coalg},\mathbin{\otimes^!},J), in the sense of Jacob Lurie, Higher Algebra, Definition 4.1.1.6. It consists of a coalgebra F∈CoalgF\in\operatorname{Coalg} and maps of coalgebras m:F⊗!F→F,u:J→F,m\colon F\mathbin{\otimes^!}F\longrightarrow F,\qquad u\colon J\longrightarrow F, with coherent associativity and unit constraints. A transverse comonoid is a coassociative coalgebra object (G,∇,e)(G,\nabla,e) of the same category, with maps of coalgebras ∇:G→G⊗!G\nabla\colon G\to G\mathbin{\otimes^!}G and e:G→Je\colon G\to J. Let FF be a transverse monoid and C∈CoalgC\in\operatorname{Coalg}. A transverse action of FF on CC is a left FF-module structure α:F⊗!C→C\alpha\colon F\mathbin{\otimes^!}C\to C in this category Lurie, Higher Algebra, Definition 4.2.1.13.

A vacuum insertion inserts the specified local identity at a selected position, compatibly with translations, collisions and the operations under consideration. A pointed action is an action together with a specified point or vacuum and its required unit compatibility. A derived action retains the action maps and their coherent homotopies in the enhanced category; it is not determined by the induced action on cohomology.

A final object, also called a terminal object, is an object ZZ in a category with mapping spaces such that Map⁡(F,Z)\operatorname{Map}(F,Z) is contractible for every object FF. For a symmetric tensor, an E2E_2 algebra can be described as an associative algebra object in the category of associative algebras, with its coherent interchange. For the symmetric convolution ⋆\star and an associative algebra AA, an action of such an FF is a module structure F⋆A→AF\star A\to A in associative algebras. The convolution centre of AA is final among these actions, with all maps and action homotopies retained. Its tensor is ⋆\star and its unit is KK. It is a different universal property from that of transverse actions on a coalgebra through ⊗!\otimes^! and JJ.

A common recipient of objects a,ba,b is an object tt with specified maps a→ta\to t and b→tb\to t. A map between two such choices must commute with both incoming maps; in a category with mapping spaces it includes the commuting homotopies and their coherences.

An ambient internal endomorphism object can classify all actions in a large coalgebra category. Requiring that the actor itself factorize, retain a marked vacuum or preserve local field operations changes the category in which finality is asked. A map from the bulk observables to an ambient endomorphism object consequently does not establish a centre theorem for the restricted actors. Even an action on a chosen boundary needs its own point and compatibility data.

Boundaries, states and the physical comparisons

A junction is a meeting of specified boundary or line conditions. Algebraically its observables can form a bimodule MM carrying compatible actions of the algebras on its two sides. Morita comparison uses such bimodules to compare module categories. A double-centralizer equivalence identifies an algebra with the derived endomorphisms of MM over the algebra acting on the other side, with the appropriate opposite multiplication.

Fusion combines adjacent defects or boundary modules by a specified relative product; an algebraic model is M⊗B𝕃NM\otimes_B^{\mathbb L}N. Sewing requires these products and evaluations to agree when intervals or surfaces are glued. An incoming cap supplies the specified map or functional at an incoming boundary end. Its coefficient domain and compatibility with gluing are part of its definition.

A field realization expresses the relevant geometric algebra or module through states, translation and operator fields, preserving the specified operations. The matrix algebra of all continuous modes can be larger than the algebra realized by local fields. Thus double-centralizer reconstruction at the mode level and local field reconstruction are separate assertions.

The BV formalism describes gauge fields, their symmetries and equations by a graded space with an odd Poisson bracket and a degree-one differential. In its quantum version an additional second-order operator Δ\Delta enters. The quantum master equation for an action SS is dS+12{S,S}+ℏΔS=0dS+\tfrac12\{S,S\}+\hbar\Delta S=0, with the stated degrees and regularization. The BFV boundary formalism equips boundary fields with their boundary symplectic and charge data so that restriction and gluing are compatible with the bulk equations.

A cyclic pairing is a specified bilinear pairing compatible with the differential and with cyclic permutation of inputs to the operations, including the degree signs. It is the extra datum that permits action functionals and gluing contractions in algebraic models. Its existence does not follow from multiplication alone.

An obstruction is a demonstrated failure of the required equation or map in the stated admissible class. A relative obstruction measures the failure of a specified comparison or extension while preserving stated boundary or normalization data. If one chosen correction cannot be homotoped to zero, another correction need not be excluded. The quantifier over admissible corrections is therefore part of every negative result below.

The geometric and arithmetic branches require additional objects—critical loci, their cohomology, and analytic test spaces. They will be defined with the computations that use them. The common distinction is already visible: an algebra, its possible representation by fields, a boundary action, and an evaluating physical state are different stages of reconstruction.

4The obstruction and the construction

The essential difficulty

We seek a reversible passage between associative descriptions of local fields—associative-to-associative chiral Koszul duality—with quantum-group rules for combining representations and reconstruction of bulk, or interior, observables from boundary data. Chiral products depend on complex positions and can have collision poles.

Over a characteristic-zero field kk, a Heisenberg current JJ with nonzero level κ\kappa and vacuum 𝟏\mathbf1 has, at positions z,wz,w,

J(z)J(w)∼κ(z−w)2𝟏.J(z)J(w)\sim\frac{\kappa}{(z-w)^2}\mathbf1.

One mode acts on k[x]k[x] by xx and b=κ∂xb=\kappa\partial_x. Taking the constant term after acting on 11 sends b,xb,x to zero but bxbx to κ\kappa. The curved bar–cobar construction retains this scalar: operators lift to degree-zero generators c(f)c(f), pairs to degree-minus-one generators c(f,g)c(f,g), with dc(b,x)=c(b)c(x)−c(xb)−κdc(b,x)=c(b)c(x)-c(xb)-\kappa. Sending c(f)c(f) to ff and longer generators to zero recovers the finite-mode algebra up to cohomology, with d2=0d^2=0.

The local vacuum acts as an identity field. A scalar augmentation preserves operations; an evaluating physical state requires further data. The empty-configuration unit joins independent insertions. For u=z−wu=z-w, R=k[[u]]R=k[[u]] and L=k((u))L=k((u)), no nonzero regular-coefficient-linear map from Laurent to regular series exists: deleting poles fails on u⋅u−1=1u\cdot u^{-1}=1. Strict binary associativity in the ordinary Beilinson–Drinfeld chiral category of a smooth curve kills triple composites; its canonical vacuum residue action then forces zero. Ordered collision complexes lie outside that strict category.

  • Fields: coefficient duals require a separate realization by fields across collisions.
  • Centre: compare the geometric object representing local actions with free coefficient operations.
  • Quantum groups: the raw diagonal tensor lacks the proposed vacuum unit; bar–cobar transport gives another tensor and unit.
  • Lines: the ordinary free algebra is augmented, but its full operations obstruct scalar augmentation; the global line consequence requires binary coefficient realization.
  • Junctions: recover both boundary actions on operators changing boundary conditions, retaining collisions and vacua.

Full coefficient duality is an equivalence reversing maps for the prescribed augmented algebras with empty coefficient kk. Marked interacting current realizations retain both orders, all collisions, coherent cuts and both vacua. Bar–cobar comparisons include compatible graded vacuum projections on flat models, relative uncurving and central Heisenberg and affine sl(2) resolutions. The native polar comparison reaches first quantum order on the full four-current vacuum; second order remains open.

The complete free junction constructed from its action on an interval times a complex disc, at scalar coupling one with whole-space and point boundaries, compares the full regular, localized and supported action diagrams on finite polynomial inputs and ordered current operations. It preserves translation, fusion, vacua and successive interval sewings. Interactions require corrections to products and both actions, compatible with collisions and sewing.

A field marking specifies jet operators recording derivative data. An operation-preserving coefficient automorphism can fail to lift with the marking fixed; transporting it gives a field isomorphism. Object realization, recovery of additional data and lifting specified maps are distinct questions.

The general unital curved comparison remains open. On a common coefficient domain, a comparison FF between products μ\mu must satisfy Fμnative≃μdual(F⊗F)F\mu_{\mathrm{native}}\simeq\mu_{\mathrm{dual}}(F\otimes F), preserving units, completions and higher collisions. Centre, line and junction maps remain separate obligations.

5A complete local reconstruction

A complete free example: reconstructing the two boundaries

The preceding definitions are meant to recover operations that can be computed independently in a field theory. A free example now does this through collisions and interval sewing. It also shows why the choice of coefficients is part of the result. The example is a rank-one cotangent theory on an interval times a complex disk. “Rank one” means that its target coordinate takes values in one copy of ℂ\mathbb C; “cotangent” means that the theory includes both that coordinate and its conjugate field.

Write t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] for the interval coordinate and z∈Uz\in U for the disk coordinate. The fields are differential forms BB and aa on the interval and disk, with aa carrying a holomorphic one-form factor and a degree shift. The quadratic action is S=∫[0,1]Tr⁡zB(dt+∂‾)a,Tr⁡zα=−12πi∫Udz∧α. S=\int_{[0,1]}\operatorname{Tr}_z B(d_t+\bar\partial)a, \qquad \operatorname{Tr}_z\alpha=-\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_U dz\wedge\alpha. Here dtd_t differentiates along the interval and ∂‾\bar\partial is the antiholomorphic differential on the disk. The action uses compact tangential support. At the left endpoint the tangential part of aa vanishes; at the right endpoint the tangential part of BB vanishes. These are respectively the whole-space and point boundary conditions. They are specified in the action before an algebra of endomorphisms is computed. The scalar coupling is one, and the local operators are finite polynomials in the stated fields, their boundary traces and selected normal integrals, with finite tangential derivatives. An arbitrary formal coupling series cannot be evaluated at one to obtain this domain.

Four projected fields carry the essential calculation. The fields γ\gamma and β\beta are even of degree zero; bb and cc are odd of degrees −1-1 and 11. The differential DD and nonzero contractions are Db=γ,Dβ=−c,Dγ=Dc=0, Db=\gamma,\qquad D\beta=-c,\qquad D\gamma=Dc=0, C(β(z),γ(w))=1z−w,C(γ(z),β(w))=−1z−w, C(\beta(z),\gamma(w))=\frac1{z-w},\qquad C(\gamma(z),\beta(w))=-\frac1{z-w}, C(c(z),b(w))=C(b(z),c(w))=1z−w. C(c(z),b(w))=C(b(z),c(w))=\frac1{z-w}. The symbol CC denotes the contraction in the free-field product. The different signs of the even and odd pairs express their respective commutator rules. They also make the differential compatible with the contractions: for instance, the two terms −C(c,b)-C(c,b) and C(β,γ)C(\beta,\gamma) cancel. Boundary coordinates have primitives among the interval integrals. Keeping these primitives, rather than taking cohomology immediately, retains the junction on which both boundaries act.

The endpoint traces give the boundary field algebras 𝒜W=ℂ[∂zjγ0:j≥0],𝒜P=Λ(∂zjc1:j≥0). \mathcal A_W=\mathbb C[\partial_z^j\gamma_0:j\geq0], \qquad \mathcal A_P=\Lambda(\partial_z^jc_1:j\geq0). The subscripts distinguish the two endpoints. Both algebras have unit 11 and no singular contraction between their own generators. On holomorphic local states the junction has the explicit complex M=ℂ[xi,yn]⊗Λ(θi,ηn),D=∑i≥0xi∂θi−∑n≥1ηn∂yn. M=\mathbb C[x_i,y_n]\otimes\Lambda(\theta_i,\eta_n), \qquad D=\sum_{i\geq0}x_i\partial_{\theta_i} -\sum_{n\geq1}\eta_n\partial_{y_n}. Here xi,θix_i,\theta_i are creation modes of γ,b\gamma,b, and yn,ηny_n,\eta_n are creation modes of β,c\beta,c, with n≥1n\geq1. Each state uses finitely many modes and has finite polynomial degree. The opposite, regular modes act by differentiation: pn=∂ynp_n=\partial_{y_n} and κi=∂θi\kappa_i=\partial_{\theta_i}. Thus the two mode algebras begin as A=ℂ[xi,pn]A=\mathbb C[x_i,p_n] and B=Λ(κi,ηn)B=\Lambda(\kappa_i,\eta_n).

The derived reconstruction uses their regular-test completions. For Â\widehat A, a row indexed by a finite regular-mode monomial has a finite polynomial output; for B̂\widehat B it has a finite exterior output. There may be infinitely many rows. These conditions distinguish the completion from arbitrary infinite sums acting on every state. The mapping categories also retain the polarization, which distinguishes the regular modes from the multiplying modes. Rationality of the regular exterior action means that each vector is killed by all sufficiently high κi\kappa_i. For the polynomial action, each vector is killed by the ideal (pn:n>N)+(p1,…,pN)h(p_n:n>N)+(p_1,\ldots,p_N)^h for some N,hN,h. The degree bound is required as well as the mode cutoff.

Here is the derived category used by the comparison. The regular actions are equivalently coactions of an exterior or polynomial coalgebra. Over ℂ\mathbb C, call a complex of such comodules coacyclic if it belongs to the smallest triangulated subcategory generated by total complexes of short exact sequences and closed under arbitrary direct sums. Forming a triangulated subcategory allows shifts and cones as well as isomorphisms. The semiderived category used here inverts a module map when its cone, after forgetting the multiplying action, is coacyclic for the regular coalgebra. For a differential graded coefficient algebra RR, the coefficient-valued comparison keeps RR-linear maps but tests this coacyclicity after forgetting RR as well. This last convention is essential for nonsplit coefficient localization sequences. The complete definition and derived action theorem supply the mapping complexes in that category.

Each actual boundary action identifies its completed algebra with the derived endomorphism object of the junction computed as a module over the other boundary. The maps preserve the unit and ordinary holomorphic translation. This is stronger than matching dimensions of cohomology: the comparison maps are the field-theoretic actions themselves. It is also a statement on a specified category. Replacing its weak equivalences or its completion changes the question.

Keeping the operation as well as its value

For a collision equation h=za−zbh=z_a-z_b, the two-term coefficient complex K(h)=[RI→−locRI[h−1]]K(h)=[R_I\xrightarrow{-\mathrm{loc}}R_I[h^{-1}]] in degrees zero and one retains the supported contribution. Tensor products of these complexes describe intersections of collision faces; their localization triangles and Mayer–Vietoris maps retain the attachments for unions. They are coefficient objects. In particular d1≠0d1\ne0, so they cannot be treated as unital coefficient algebras without changing the construction.

To retain the operations on these coefficients, use the Dolbeault resolution by pseudomeromorphic currents on a smooth polydisk. These currents admit the particular principal-value and residue operations needed here. For a nonzero holomorphic denominator gg, denote those operators by PgP_g and RgR_g. They are defined by analytic continuation from |g|2λ/g|g|^{2\lambda}/g and ∂‾|g|2λ/g\bar\partial|g|^{2\lambda}/g, respectively, and satisfy [∂‾,Pg]=Rg,[∂‾,Rg]=0.[\bar\partial,P_g]=R_g,\qquad[\bar\partial,R_g]=0. Their order matters. For positive integers m,p,qm,p,q, put rm(u)=∂‾PV⁡(u−m)r_m(u)=\bar\partial\operatorname{PV}(u^{-m}). Then RupPuq(1)=rp+q(u),PuqRup(1)=0.R_{u^p}P_{u^q}(1)=r_{p+q}(u),\qquad P_{u^q}R_{u^p}(1)=0. The first operation divides before taking a residue. Remembering only the final supported value of a residue would lose this distinction. The coefficient diagram therefore retains finite words in PgP_g and RgR_g, together with their differential and actual composition.

Root identifications are derived along with the operation algebra. For independent equations a1,…,aca_1,\ldots,a_c imposing a root identification, use the finite Koszul complex with degree −1-1 generators ϵj\epsilon_j and differential dϵj=ajd\epsilon_j=a_j. It retains the normal directions that ordinary substitution would erase. An operation label remains on this complex even when its denominator becomes zero after root identification; it is a transported operation, not a request to divide by zero on the smaller space. Successive root identifications compare through tensor products of their Koszul complexes. This is where the attachments and their signs enter the composition law.

The same distinction appears at three points. With a=u−va=u-v, 1ua=1va−1uv.\frac1{ua}=\frac1{va}-\frac1{uv}. For the left-hand fraction, taking the scalar Laurent residue first in uu and then in vv gives −1-1; first in vv and then in uu gives 00; first in aa and then in vv gives +1+1. These are coefficient extractions. Current residues also carry the sign from reordering their differential forms. The relation retains all three channels; a claim that two projected channels agree would discard the third. The full diagram includes nonconsecutive mergers such as 13∣213\mid2, with the second input still present. The complete collision construction supplies both the coefficient complexes and the ordered operations on them.

What the complete comparison proves

On each specified collection of polynomial inputs, Wick expansion has finitely many labeled contractions and a finite pole bound. A contraction pairs two field slots, and unpaired slots remain in the normal product. Both orders of an iterated Wick product enumerate the same complete matchings, with the same permutation signs for odd fields. This proves compatibility of the native field comparison with its actual operations. At a collision the coefficients use the monic lattice, the current diagram and the derived root maps just described.

The coefficient-valued action theorem keeps the source junction fixed. Over a commutative differential graded ℂ\mathbb C-algebra RR, that source is MR=R⊗ℂMM_R=R\otimes_{\mathbb C}M. For a coefficient complex VV of RR-modules, the target is MV=V⊗ℂMM_V=V\otimes_{\mathbb C}M, and the derived maps run from MRM_R to MVM_V. They are not obtained by declaring VV to be its own endomorphism algebra. The theorem is natural in homogeneous maps of VV, including the principal-value/residue differential action, and preserves the finite localization, support and root complexes. This naturality assembles the individual action comparisons into one equivalence of diagrams.

Disjoint fusion requires one more ingredient than the Chinese remainder splitting of test spaces: changing the creation splitting introduces a Gaussian whose coefficients are the cross-residue pairings. Its exponential is finite on every polynomial state because each contraction lowers occupation by two. Transverse interval sewing has independently specified seam fields. Its comparison uses the module Gaussian and the inverse auxiliary Gaussian, with the full boundary units retained. The simultaneous seam calculation makes successive sewings compatible with disjoint fusion and collision transport.

The resulting theorem is a complete local boundary-junction comparison for this free rank-one theory, at scalar coupling one, on the finite polynomial and current-word domain. It includes both derived actions, regular and supported coefficients, all ordered label partitions, normal derivatives, translation, disjoint fusion and successive interval sewing. It therefore gives a positive model of the requested reconstruction, rather than merely an algebra with the expected character.

The first interacting extension asks for an independently defined deformation of this same physical system. Its boundary conditions, junction differential and action maps must be specified again. One must then show which part of the free contraction and matching argument survives and solve the new compatibility equation where it fails. Arbitrary singular observables, formal coupling completion and Ramond fields also require further comparison theorems. None is contained in the free theorem’s quantifiers. The question is whether the retained operations extend together on a natural larger domain.
