Recovering the algebra from its collision coefficients

The first result is a reconstruction on the chosen geometric carrier. Write 𝒞\mathcal C for the category of coherent coefficient systems on the ordered collision atlas, ⋆\star for its convolution, and E1E_1 for homotopy-coherent associativity. The empty coefficient is fixed to kk.

Proved at the stated hypotheses

The geometric bar and cobar are inverse

Here 𝒞\mathcal C is the enhanced category on the ordered collision atlas, with convolution ⋆\star and empty unit KK. The subscript E1E_1 specifies coherent associativity. Both empty coefficients are kk; the reduced terms are positive.

The functors BB and Ω\Omega induce inverse equivalences Alg⁡E1aug,A⌀=k(𝒞,⋆)≃Coalg⁡E1coaug,C⌀=k(𝒞,⋆).\operatorname{Alg}^{\mathrm{aug},\,A_\varnothing=k}_{E_1}(\mathcal C,\star) \simeq \operatorname{Coalg}^{\mathrm{coaug},\,C_\varnothing=k}_{E_1}(\mathcal C,\star). The coalgebras are homotopy-coherent counital coassociative coalgebras. No additional global elementwise conilpotence assumption is needed.

To see why the comparison is an equivalence, flatten an iterated bar–cobar word into its original factors. Each gap is either inside one block or between two blocks. In the associated graded complex, changing that choice is an identity map between consecutive degrees. The complex of all choices is a tensor product of two-term identity complexes, so it contracts unless there is just one original factor. That factor and the empty term recover the original object. At nn labels there are at most nn factors; the filtration is finite there. This proves the result without imposing a uniform bound on cohomological degrees.

The same finite argument works for the word cut product. There it has a particularly explicit support consequence. Recall the locus ZnZ_n at which every consecutive cut is crossed by an equality.

Proved at the stated hypotheses

The support of the word cobar in every arity

Let XX be smooth, separated, of finite type and positive pure dimension over a characteristic-zero field. Work in the word carrier 𝒲X\mathcal W_X, with the strong cut coproducts and full-cut loci ZnZ_n defined above. The reduced term has zero empty coefficient.

For a strong cut coalgebra CC, there is a natural equivalence of positive word coefficient systems ΩcutC¯n≃RΓZn(Cn)[−1].\begin{equation} \overline{\Omega_{\mathrm{cut}}C}_n \simeq R\Gamma_{Z_n}(C_n)[-1]. \end{equation} It commutes with monotone collisions and coalgebra morphisms. Its composite with RΓZn(Cn)[−1]→Cn[−1]R\Gamma_{Z_n}(C_n)[-1]\to C_n[-1] is the length-one projection.

The proof identifies the iterated coproduct diagram with the localization cube of the opens UpU_p. Its nonempty vertices give the Čech complex of their union. Adjoining the empty vertex takes the fibre of restriction to that union, which is local cohomology on its complement ZnZ_n. The cobar desuspension supplies the shift [−1][-1]. The inverse factorization maps on the opens also give the multiplication; the supported object alone would not determine it.

Proved at the stated hypotheses

Factorization is equivalent to full-cut support

An augmented cut algebra is ZZ-supported when its positive arity-nn coefficient is supported on ZnZ_n. Empty coefficients are fixed to kk. The strong condition concerns each consecutive-cut component, and the categories retain coherent maps.

With the empty coefficient fixed to kk, bar and cobar restrict to inverse equivalences Alg⁡E1aug,Z(𝒲X)⇄BcutΩcutCoalg⁡E1coaug,strong(𝒲X).\operatorname{Alg}_{E_1}^{\mathrm{aug},Z}(\mathcal W_X) \ \underset{\Omega_{\mathrm{cut}}}{\overset{B_{\mathrm{cut}}} {\rightleftarrows}}\ \operatorname{Coalg}_{E_1}^{\mathrm{coaug},\mathrm{strong}}(\mathcal W_X). These are full subcategories of the ambient enhanced categories, so the equivalence includes their mapping spaces.

This identifies a natural domain of associative algebras in every arity. Small-diagonal support is a further restriction. On an equality stratum in ZnZ_n with more than one equality block, the extra condition is vanishing of the extraordinary restriction of CnC_n. At three labels this tests the outer collision with the middle point distinct. A binary comparison cannot decide that vanishing: there are coefficient systems whose first two terms vanish and whose third term is supported precisely on that extra stratum.

The small-diagonal restriction has another consequence. For a right differential module MM on a smooth dd-dimensional space, let i(M[d−1])i(M[d-1]) be its insertion on every small diagonal. Its associative cut structures form a discrete space, and both composites of its binary product vanish. On a curve this follows from the two-channel residue relation; in higher dimension it follows from the local-cohomology sum of the two channel submodules. This is the precise two-step nilpotence theorem for a uniformly shifted module in the heart. A coefficient complex with larger full-cut support lies outside its hypotheses. Diagonal rigidity and its higher-dimensional extension state that boundary.

A positive comparison between the two geometric carriers requires additional exchange data. For each pair of order charts σ,ρ\sigma,\rho, give an equivalence gσρg_{\sigma\rho} on their full overlap, with coherent Čech cocycles, relabelings and ordered-fibre collision maps. These overlaps contain partial collisions. For a cut coalgebra, require that the comparisons commute with every separated block coproduct and its refinements. With 𝒞X\mathcal C_X denoting the atlas systems, the result is:

Theorem — proved with the complete exchange datum

Descent from words with exchange on full overlaps

The word and atlas carriers, their charts and all-subset convolution are defined above. Full-overlap exchange means the specified chart equivalences with all Čech, relabeling and ordered-fibre collision coherences; factorization compatibility retains every separated coproduct and refinement.

Restriction identifies 𝒞X\mathcal C_X with the category of word systems carrying exchange data on full overlaps. Its tensor product is the all-subset convolution, glued chartwise. Under this equivalence, componentwise strong collision coalgebras correspond to strong cut coalgebras with factorization-compatible exchange data.

The proof glues the coefficient modules by descent, then glues their collision maps and mapping spaces. On a cross-disjoint open, reorder the blocks until they are consecutive; factorization compatibility makes the resulting coproduct independent of that choice. This constructs the inverse, including higher coherences.

Exchange need not exist on a fixed system. If a cut algebra has positive ideal Δn,*M\Delta_{n,*}M and nonzero separated external square, its bar has zero restriction to x1=x3≠x2x_1=x_3\ne x_2 in chart 123123 and nonzero two-word restriction in chart 132132. Those restrictions lie on a common chart overlap, so no exchange can identify them. Nevertheless interval-word inclusion gives a structured bar map, and interval-word projection gives a structured cobar map. The role of physical order is also delimited. For scalar local systems on real collision chambers, compatible paths give the all-arity chamber comparison, retaining both half-braid directions and their concatenations. The extension to dg coefficients and the current comparison use their stated extra hypotheses. An ordered word, an order in a collision fibre, and a time-ordered physical correlation function are three objects with comparison maps between them. The bar theorem alone does not identify all three.

Cocommutative factorization identifies these products on common refinements, so they glue with all collision maps, normal derivatives and both units. The mixed triple (a,−a,a)(a,-a,a) retains the 1313 contact and treats position two as a separated spectator. The symmetric reconstruction proves the functorial comparison.

Regular nonidentity exchange admits a different positive construction. For the residue coalgebras of rational quantum vertex algebras, there is also a precise relation between atlas and word constructions. Recognizing an arbitrary object of the atlas heart as one of these field realizations requires compatibility in every arity. A three-input condition alone is insufficient.

Proved at the stated hypotheses

The supported vacuum obstruction survives convention changes

Which universal centre exists?

There are two positive universal constructions before any factorizing restriction is imposed. For the symmetric convolution category 𝒞R\mathcal C_R, let Act⁡(A)\operatorname{Act}(A) be the category of E2E_2 actions on an associative algebra AA defined above. Theorem — proved in the symmetric convolution category

The universal centre for convolution actions

Here RR is a commutative coefficient algebra, 𝒞R\mathcal C_R is the presentable stable atlas coefficient category with symmetric convolution ⋆\star, and AA is an associative algebra for that tensor. An action is an E2E_2 actor with a left module structure on AA in associative algebras. The action category and its mapping spaces retain all unit and comparison homotopies. The bimodule mapping functor in the statement is defined on this same category.

Let AA be an algebra of (𝒞R,⋆)(\mathcal C_R,\star).

Its underlying object represents V↦Map⁡A−A(V⋆A,A)V\mapsto\operatorname{Map}_{A-A}(V\star A,A). The construction of this internal bimodule Hom gives existence, and the coherent composition operations give its E2E_2 structure. Evaluating on the unit of AA gives the stated algebra map to AA. This theorem concerns convolution actions on algebras.

This is a positive closed-category construction. Imposing factorization on every actor produces a different universal problem; the ambient endomorphism coalgebra need not belong to that smaller category.

The strongest ordinary-carrier result applies over ℂ\mathbb C on the affine line. Admit all connected, coaugmented, counital factorizing coassociative coalgebras with coherent unital transverse monoid structure as actors; action morphisms retain the units and all comparison homotopies.

Proved at the stated hypotheses

No final ordinary factorizing monoid actor with a nonzero derivation

Work over ℂ\mathbb C on the affine line with algebraic QQ in degree zero. Admit all connected factorizing coassociative coalgebras with coherent unital transverse monoid structure as actors on CQC_Q, retaining every action-comparison homotopy. No augmentation to JJ or propagation condition is added.

If QQ admits a nonzero vertex derivation, its category of native monoid actions has no final object. More precisely, there are two parallel morphisms of monoid actions which no receiving factorizing monoid action can equalize up to homotopy. The assertion allows unbounded derived receiving actors.

The detector is a parallel pair of maps of monoid actions. A receiving map would have to kill a binary class, but one part of that class is detected by a nonzero singleton derivation and the other by the vacuum. They occupy different cohomological bidegrees and cannot cancel. The proof permits unbounded derived receiving actors. It applies to Heisenberg whenever a nonzero vertex derivation is chosen, and to the stated affine examples. For the unit vertex algebra ℂ\mathbb C, the derivations vanish and the final actor is instead JJ.

Two distinctions survive the negative theorem. First, parallel maps that cannot be equalized after any receiving map do not imply two objects with no common recipient. The category with two objects a,ba,b and precisely two arrows a⇉ba\rightrightarrows b illustrates the difference: every pair of objects has common recipient bb, but there is no final object. Second, geometric actors need not all arise from physical bulk theories.

Proved at the stated hypotheses

When a physical universal property transfers to geometric actions

Junction reconstruction and the locality of its maps

The junction approach begins with a bimodule and asks what algebra acts from either side. On the graded, completed oscillator domain, the reverse map

Evaluation on line modules has an exact finite-orbit criterion. Quantization retains more than the action of derivations

A coisson algebra is the classical chiral Poisson structure: a commutative differential algebra with a singular Lie bracket satisfying the translation, skew-symmetry, Jacobi and Leibniz identities. In one coordinate the singular bracket is encoded by the polynomial λ\lambda-bracket {aλb}\{a_\lambda b\}. A deformation quantization is a flat formal deformation whose commutator, divided by its parameter and reduced at parameter zero, recovers that Poisson bracket, with the corresponding operation identities.

The Poisson vertex sigma model uses this classical structure to construct a field theory holomorphic in one direction and topological in specified real directions. “Topological” means invariance under the allowed deformations of positions in those directions. Its boundary and line observables are different recipients. A proposed comparison must carry their products and gauge equations, not just their cohomology dimensions.

For matrix models, constants can retain the rank. Passing from Hamiltonian functions to derivations quotients out constants, so a derivation action can survive when a prescribed Hamiltonian lift does not. The coefficient-Weyl deformation parameter and the parameter quantizing matrix coordinates are also distinct: inverting the former can contract a finite unframed complex without constructing the latter quantization. There are finite all-arity derivation actions, BRST homotopies, framed models, local quantum Hamiltonian maps and an integral local reduction with a BFV comparison arrow. The global prescribed-charge and framing-adic extensions have their own obstructions. An arrow must still be proved a quasi-isomorphism if an equivalence is claimed.

A cyclic model must additionally retain the trace data. A mixed complex (C,b,B)(C,b,B) has operators satisfying b2=B2=bB+Bb=0b^2=B^2=bB+Bb=0. In cochain convention |b|=1|b|=1 and |B|=−1|B|=-1. Its negative cyclic complex is (C[[u]],b+uB)(C[[u]],b+uB), where |u|=2|u|=2 so the differential has degree one. Its classes can encode the cyclic structures needed for a Calabi–Yau pairing. A product-preserving map need not preserve that class.

Several newer comparisons sharpen these questions. The fixed-ring metric calculation identifies a nonzero one-dimensional cohomology class and excludes the stated metric lift even after allowing all connections in its fixed coefficient class. The ramified-parameter model already has a Cartan homotopy over ℂ[a]\mathbb C[a], including the required symmetry; realizing that homotopy by the desired geometry remains separate. The nilpotent-flux extension admits the prescribed global Lie section exactly when its flux vanishes. These are statements about specified lifts, not failures of every algebraic or physical description.

For Neumann mixed strings, the staggered resolvent gives uniform cutoff inverses and convergent Gaussian responses. Heat and rational insertion homotopies, supported primitives for finite contacts and a two-normal corner homotopy are constructed. The ordinary Sobolev determinant comparison is also proved on its stated domain. The finite-segment scalar heat comparison uses tests supported in (−∞,L)2(-\infty,L)^2. These operations still need comparison with an independently defined local cyclic BV–BFV regulator and its residual quantum measure. Both normal-source insertions and the boundary/corner terms must survive that comparison.

Cyclic words map to collective Moyal operators

Matrix traces retain the cyclic order of their factors. Reducing a matrix moment constraint can identify different orders, but the identification has quantum corrections. An all-word comparison is available on polynomial coefficients, including the coproduct. Its proof constructs the reduced expressions first and uses all-rank faithfulness only afterward.

Classical restriction is a global quasi-isomorphism. For the traceless matrices, the eight commutator equations generate an ideal of height six. Hamiltonian comparison: the coupled operation equations

A cochain equivalence between classical and quantized observables need not preserve their products and brackets. Even after separate binary homotopies have been found, the Leibniz relation couples those homotopies. Nonclosed inputs expose this coupling: their differentials contribute to the same equation. Continuous Hamiltonian cochains provide an explicit reduction of the full comparison problem and positive constructions on several domains.

Flat and curved representatives

Three propagators lead to different presentations of the genus-dependent bar construction: a rational local propagator, a holomorphic prime-form propagator on the universal cover, and a single-valued Arakelov propagator. The first two presentations have square-zero differentials. The Arakelov presentation has a degree-one operator dArd_{\mathrm{Ar}} with square dAr2=κωgd_{\mathrm{Ar}}^2=\kappa\omega_g, where ωg\omega_g is the curvature operator. When this product is nonzero, ordinary cochain cohomology is unavailable for that presentation.

The distinction persists under every invertible degree-zero operator TT on a common graded carrier:

(T−1dT)2=T−1d2T.(T^{-1}dT)^2=T^{-1}d^2T.

Consequently an ordinary gauge conjugation cannot identify either flat differential with the genuinely curved one. A formal exponential that transports the square of an already curved differential preserves this distinction. It does not construct a chain map from a flat complex to a curved complex.

A comparison may instead be formulated in a specified category of curved objects. The conditional flat-derived and curved-coderived comparison requires a constructed curvature-compatible morphism whose associated graded is the identity and an actual well-defined cone satisfying the bounded filtered acyclicity criterion. The higher-genus application also retains its chiral Riemann–Hilbert hypothesis. Under those assumptions the cone is coacyclic and the morphism becomes invertible in the coderived category. The first missing construction is the typed morphism and its cone; formal invertibility of the exponential and a curvature-square identity alone supply neither. This conditional comparison leaves both flat derived presentations and the curved Arakelov presentation available with their respective operations.

How the constructions fit together

The free junction gives one route through the programme: an action determines boundary fields; the fields determine collision operations; the junction carries the two boundary actions; and the derived comparison respects fusion and sewing. Other examples begin at different points. A quantum group may first be given by generators and a coproduct. A Hall algebra begins with spaces of extensions. An arithmetic state begins with an evaluation on a specified test algebra. The common problem is to construct the maps between these independently defined objects, with the operations that their next use requires.

This gives a precise distinction between an object, additional structure on it, and a comparison. A complex may have the correct cohomology yet lack a specified exchange. An algebra may admit several choices of state–field marking. Two marked objects may be isomorphic through a map that moves the marking, although no isomorphism preserves a fixed marking. An equivalence of complexes becomes an equivalence of field systems only after its compatibility with products, translation, vacua and collisions is established. The coefficient automorphism example and the free junction exhibit the negative and positive sides of this distinction.

The comparison maps determine their common domain

The geometric constructions give two associative reconstructions, one on the full collision atlas and one on ordered words with consecutive cuts. Full-overlap exchange identifies atlas coefficient systems with word systems carrying that additional datum. The algebra comparison passes through the coalgebra:

A↦Ωcutres⁡ordcoBatA.A\longmapsto \Omega_{\mathrm{cut}}\operatorname{res}^{\mathrm{co}}_{\mathrm{ord}} B_{\mathrm{at}}A.

Each arrow has its own tensor and support condition. The outer-collision coefficient can distinguish the resulting cut algebra from literal restriction of the atlas algebra. Normalized étale extension provides another actual coalgebra comparison: it reconstructs newly separated block coefficients and identifies the strong bar of the normalized word pullback. Its separate three-run covering obstruction shows why functorial reconstruction and descent must be proved independently.

Two kinds of duality then use these coefficient systems. Full transposition reverses the arrows and exchanges open extensions in its declared pro-perfect recipient; it can produce a second associative algebra on transported coefficients. Marked normal inversion is a covariant reconstruction using a specified punctured coefficient and its attachment. Its native tensor, transfer, residue and vacuum comparisons are part of the equivalence. A physical regular lattice may map through a strict span of different quotients, as the weight-one example demonstrates. Comparing these two routes requires their actual coefficients and operations on a common domain.

Operation homotopies decide how far a complex comparison can be used. In the continuous Hamiltonian problem, one common family satisfies the binary equations and several mixed equations while retaining the same lower operations, parameter precision and finite input refinements. Its complementary mixed residual remains coupled to the two unsolved binary residuals. In the relative rank-three matrix problem, the quantum cohomology algebras already agree, yet a nonzero invariant four-argument class excludes the fixed strict Cartan recipient. These are different source and recipient categories. The relative obstruction does not settle the continuous Hamiltonian comparison or the absolute reconstruction problem with positive ghosts.

The same discipline connects the geometric constructions to quantum groups and physical observables. Finite-current probes can reconstruct an adic representation system with genuine polar exchange, and the effective finite coend has a precise rank criterion inside its completion. A duality-closed evaluation category can still have no ordinary braiding while retaining a rigid tensor comparison and meromorphic interchange. The exchange domain is therefore part of any geometric representation equivalence. For physical reconstruction, the free junction supplies an action-to-fields-to-collisions route with its native boundary actions and sewing. A geometric actor, however, becomes a physical observable only through the independently specified field, state and boundary maps.

Hall and arithmetic realizations provide further independently defined inputs to this network. Their coefficient functors must preserve the native extension correspondences, orientations, support and parameter directions; their states must act on the full prescribed test domain. A trace, character or index can then be a consequence of a comparison, but it does not supply the missing object, operation or sewing map. The examples below retain both the constructed recipients and these exact remaining arrows.

Geometry, duality and the second algebra

The first geometric choice concerns which collisions the object records. The word carrier orders the insertions and supports its cut product. The full collision atlas keeps a larger system of collision charts and their overlaps. A transverse real direction has a third meaning: it orders the composition of physical regions along intervals. A comparison between these geometries has to preserve the relevant collision and sewing maps. A word order alone does not identify the corresponding physical intervals, and a comparison that exists away from collisions need not extend through them.

On the declared geometric domains, bar and cobar reconstruct an associative algebra from its coalgebra of collision coefficients. Transposing the full coefficient diagram then gives a second associative algebra in the specified pro-perfect recipient. These are distinct steps. Bar–cobar is an equivalence between algebra and coalgebra descriptions; coefficient duality reverses variance and changes the coefficient recipient. A covariant state–field realization of the second algebra is a further construction. The marked charged-current realization proves that this further step can succeed with genuine noncommutative products.

The comparison with Lie–commutative chiral duality enters on its own domain. The Francis–Gaitsgory construction relates chiral Lie data and commutative factorization coalgebras. Its relation to associative envelopes explains an important class of examples; it does not supply the general associative-to-associative field comparison. The nonlinear spin-three and charged-current examples prevent the second associative algebra from being declared universally commutative. Conversely, their existence does not identify every coefficient dual with a field algebra.

The internal dual seen by a line has yet another definition. Its tensor and its vacuum requirements must be compared with those of the coefficient and field duals. Several prescribed vacuum-preserving comparisons are obstructed. The result identifies the incompatible requirements in those comparison classes. It does not make the dual objects disappear, nor exclude a comparison with explicitly changed coefficients, units or preserved operations. The duality questions retain the exact next field-realization problems.

b(va⊗wb)=(−1)abwb⊗va,a,b∈{0,1}. b(v_a\otimes w_b)=(-1)^{ab}w_b\otimes v_a, \qquad a,b\in\{0,1\}.

If pp projects onto E1E_1 and τ\tau is the ordinary flip, then b=τ(1−2p⊠p)b=\tau(1-2p\boxtimes p). The projector is recovered from diagonal exchange itself:

p=12(1E−Tr⁡2(Δ*b)). p=\frac12\left(1_E-\operatorname{Tr}_2(\Delta^*b)\right).

Here Δ\Delta is the diagonal and Tr⁡2\operatorname{Tr}_2 is ordinary partial trace over the second tensor factor. The identity Tr⁡2(τ(A⊗B))=BA\operatorname{Tr}_2(\tau(A\otimes B))=BA proves the formula. Moreover every exchange-intertwining map, including a noninvertible one, preserves this parity over a reduced complex base. For a vector v=v0+v1v=v_0+v_1, the equation b(v⊗v)−v⊗v=−2v1⊗v1b(v\otimes v)-v\otimes v=-2v_1\otimes v_1 recovers the even subspace; the analogous equation recovers the odd subspace. This is the intrinsic recognition and fullness theorem.

Parity-preserving maps in two different positions automatically intertwine sign exchange. Flat bundles and their horizontal projectors descend along arbitrary étale covering families. Applying the incidence construction therefore gives effective descent of the full marked sign sector, including its mapping spaces and supported operations. On disconnected curves the mixed exchanges are fixed by the recovered parity. In contrast, arbitrary regular particle data can have identical restrictions on each component and inequivalent mixed exchanges; the disjoint-cover counterexample remains valid in that larger category. For a fixed finite abelian group of colors and a symmetric sign-valued bicharacter—a pairing multiplicative in each color—descent also holds when the color projectors are retained as markings; exchange alone need not recover those labels.

The reduced-base hypothesis matters. Over D=ℂ[η]/(η2)D=\mathbb C[\eta]/(\eta^2), multiplication by η\eta from an even line to an odd line intertwines their exchanges because 2η2=02\eta^2=0. It does not preserve parity. The nilpotent-base example prevents extending unmarked fullness to such coefficient families without another argument.

Both unit objects can be included componentwise. Choose an open-and-closed subset U⊂TU\subset T, use the marked particle system on UU, and use the empty cut object on its complement. Mixed positive-arity coefficients vanish whenever one input lies in that complement. The choices (⌀,0)(\varnothing,0) and (T,0)(T,0) give KTK_T and JTJ_T, respectively. The unit extension descends and preserves both objects. Transport by cut bar–cobar gives Gf=ΩcutΨfBcutG_f=\Omega_{\mathrm{cut}}\Psi_fB_{\mathrm{cut}}, retaining the complete bar-side exchange and vacuum marking. It preserves KK and ΩcutJ\Omega_{\mathrm{cut}}J separately. No closure of this square-zero sector under the ambient transported tensor is asserted.

The normalized extension below constructs a strong target bar for an independently specified factorizing associative word algebra. Its covering-family comparison has a nonzero three-run obstruction on the full category. The marked parity construction gives effective descent on its own full incidence sector because its mixed-root operations are reconstructed there.

Normalized extension constructs a larger bar comparison

There is also an all-arity construction on the full word carrier, before imposing particle presentations. Work with unbounded quasicoherent right differential modules on ordered words, allowing repeated positions, and the cut convolution with empty unit KK. A factorizing associative word algebra has positive coefficients supported where the word admits no separated cut. Its cut bar is strong precisely under this support condition; the finite cube of cuts proves the assertion in each word length.

For an étale map f:Y→Xf:Y\to X, let v:V(f)↪Y•v:V(f)\hookrightarrow Y^{\bullet} denote the collision-reflecting open in each word length. The normalized pullback of an associative object is

GfA=K⊕N[−1],BcutGfA=⨁ℓ=0dN⋆cutℓ.G_fA=K\oplus N[-1],\qquad B_{\mathrm{cut}}G_fA=\bigoplus_{\ell=0}^dN^{\star_{\mathrm{cut}}\ell}.

This bound belongs to the displayed square-zero example. Its new separated coefficients show why the reconstructed bar is not raw inverse image.

The positive vacuum has a different comparison. Put Lf=Tf(JX)L_f=T_f(J_X). Its natural map λ:JY→Lf\lambda:J_Y\to L_f has cofiber RΓY•\WJY[1]R\Gamma_{Y^{\bullet}\setminus W}J_Y[1] and is an equivalence exactly when ff is universally injective. Ordinary covering-family descent still fails on the full category. A nonzero three-run coefficient can disappear on both members of a suitable two-open cover of the curve. Any restriction agreeing with ordinary open restriction retains this witness. The normalized étale bar theorem thus constructs objectwise pullback and its strong bar without proving descent for every word algebra. The full marked parity sector above has its stronger effective descent theorem because its mixed-root data are independently controlled.

Module duality has several precise domains

A module describes how an algebra acts on another object. Duality of algebras therefore raises a further question: which representations correspond, and which operations on representations survive? There are positive answers on geometric and field domains, with different coefficient and mapping conditions.

For geometric modules, retain a root while the other insertions move and collide. In the word geometry, let AA be an augmented associative algebra with empty coefficient equal to the ground ring, and put C=BcutAC=B_{\mathrm{cut}}A. Twisting the rooted cut product by the canonical bar twisting map τ\tau gives the rooted comodule C⋆*,τMC\star_{*,\tau}M of an AA-module MM. Full coefficient transposition then gives

M↦(C⋆*,τM)♯. M\longmapsto (C\star_{*,\tau}M)^\sharp.

The rooted duality theorem makes this an anti-equivalence with modules over C♯C^\sharp in the specified pro-coefficient category. It reverses maps and transposes the action. The root is retained, the reduced length at each finite moving configuration is bounded, and the pro-diagram of perfect coefficient stages is part of the target.

There is also a two-sided construction on the full collision atlas. Put CA=B⋆AC_A=B_\star A and 𝒦(A)=CA♯\mathcal K(A)=C_A^\sharp. For an AA–BB bimodule MM, the two-sided twisted bar is CA⋆M⋆CBC_A\star M\star C_B, and its coefficient dual is denoted 𝒦A,B(M)\mathscr K_{A,B}(M). The interface theorem gives coherent equivalences

𝒦A,D(M⋆B𝕃N)≃𝒦A,B(M)⋆♯,𝒦(B)𝕃𝒦B,D(N). \mathscr K_{A,D}(M\star_B^{\mathbb L}N) \simeq\mathscr K_{A,B}(M) \star^{\mathbb L}_{\sharp,\mathcal K(B)}\mathscr K_{B,D}(N).

The balanced product on the left composes interfaces along their shared algebra BB. On bar objects it is computed by derived cotensor; transposition gives the relative tensor on the right. Identity bimodules, all ordered collision comparisons and the associativity homotopies are retained. An exterior fusion tensor of field representations is a separately defined operation. Identifying that tensor with this balanced composition requires a comparison of its actions and coefficients.

Relative fusion can leave the domain of ordinary supported duality

The pro-object in the interface theorem has a concrete purpose. Work over k=ℂk=\mathbb C in one normal coordinate uu, with differential operators D=k⟨u,∂⟩/(∂u−u∂−1)D=k\langle u,\partial\rangle/(\partial u-u\partial-1). The right module P=D/uDP=D/uD has basis βm=[u−m−1]\beta_m=[u^{-m-1}], for m≥0m\geq0, and actions βmu=βm−1\beta_m u=\beta_{m-1} and βm∂=(m+1)βm+1\beta_m\partial=(m+1)\beta_{m+1}, with β−1=0\beta_{-1}=0. A normal support condition requires every cohomology class of a right DD-complex to be killed by some power of uu; that power may depend on the class. There is no completion in uu.

For a complex of ground spaces EE, put I(E)=P⊗kEI(E)=P\otimes_k E. The normal reconstruction identifies all supported complexes with these objects. Its inverse is RHom⁡D(P,M)=[M→⋅uM]R\operatorname{Hom}_D(P,M)=[M\xrightarrow{\cdot u}M], in degrees zero and one. Define the ordinary normal dual by 𝔻(M)=RHom⁡D(M,D)t[1]\mathbb D(M)=R\operatorname{Hom}_D(M,D)^t[1], where t(u)=ut(u)=u and t(∂)=−∂t(\partial)=-\partial convert left modules to right modules. The degreewise criterion is exact: 𝔻(I(E))\mathbb D(I(E)) is supported if and only if every Hj(E)H^j(E) is finite dimensional. In that case it is I(E∨)I(E^\vee), where E∨=RHom⁡k(E,k)E^\vee=R\operatorname{Hom}_k(E,k).

Binary tensor and dual closure impose a stronger condition. A scalar perfect ground complex is quasi-isomorphic to a bounded complex of finite-dimensional ground spaces. These form the largest class closed under scalar duals and binary tensor for which the ordinary normal dual stays supported. Indeed,

H0(E⊗E∨)=⨁jHj(E)⊗Hj(E)* H^0(E\otimes E^\vee)=\bigoplus_j H^j(E)\otimes H^j(E)^*

must be finite dimensional, forcing only finitely many nonzero cohomology groups. The perfect-ground theorem also proves the converse.

Relative fusion can violate this condition even when the starting ground spaces are finite. Let B=k[ϵ]/(ϵ2)B=k[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2) and give kk its augmentation module structure. The actual two-sided bar has zero normalized differential and gives

T=k⊗B𝕃k=⨁n≥0k[n]. T=k\otimes_B^{\mathbb L}k=\bigoplus_{n\geq0}k[n].

Here k[n]k[n] lies in degree −n-n. In the neutral Heisenberg realization 𝒩(E)=Vκ⊗E\mathcal N(E)=V_\kappa\otimes E, with κ≠0\kappa\ne0, the Ward fusion is 𝒩(E)⊠𝒩(F)=𝒩(E⊗F)\mathcal N(E)\boxtimes\mathcal N(F)=\mathcal N(E\otimes F); its unit is the full vacuum module VκV_\kappa, and its level stays κ\kappa. The supported product P⊗∏nkP\otimes\prod_n k is smaller than WW: its elements have a common normal-order bound. Replacing WW by that product changes evaluation. Retaining the inverse system ⋯→P⊕3→P⊕2→P\cdots\to P^{\oplus3}\to P^{\oplus2}\to P instead gives a valid pro-perfect dual, with ambient limit WW. Dualizing the relative bar gives a pro-cosimplicial totalization with transposed faces, actions and variance. Realizing it by native supported fields with the required physical probes is a further comparison.

A useful sufficient domain for ordinary relative fusion is homological smoothness: the intermediate algebra CC must be perfect as a module over C⊗CopC\otimes C^{\mathrm{op}}. Then scalar perfect right and left CC-modules have scalar perfect relative tensor. Alternatively, one module can be perfect over CC and the other over the scalars. Scalar perfection of CC alone does not suffice; the dual-number diagonal has an infinite alternating resolution. Over R=k[[ℏ]]R=k[[\hbar]], the analogous maximal class is Perf⁡(R)\operatorname{Perf}(R) for derived-complete grounds and completed tensor, as the formal theorem proves by reduction to the special fibre. Perfection need not imply flatness: the two characters 0,ℏ0,\hbar of R[t]R[t] have relative tensor [R→−ℏR][−1,0]≃k[R\xrightarrow{-\hbar}R]_{[-1,0]}\simeq k.

A field equivalence can depend on which maps are inverted

For the Heisenberg algebra, work over R=k[κ]R=k[\kappa] in characteristic zero. A smooth Heisenberg module has operators JnJ_n, for n∈ℤn\in\mathbb Z, satisfying [Jm,Jn]=κmδm+n,0[J_m,J_n]=\kappa m\delta_{m+n,0}; every vector is killed by all sufficiently large positive modes. On the curved side, the modes of a degree-one odd field cc anticommute. Write ξn=c(−n−1)\xi_n=c_{(-n-1)} for n≥0n\geq0 and ιm=c(m−1)\iota_m=c_{(m-1)} for m≥1m\geq1. Its degree-one operator obeys

Q2=κ∑m≥1mξmιm. Q^2=\kappa\sum_{m\geq1}m\xi_m\iota_m.

The sum is finite on each vector. Maps commuting with the modes form a complex with differential Df=Q′f−(−1)|f|fQDf=Q'f-(-1)^{|f|}fQ: its square is the commutator with this common curvature, hence zero.

The kernel construction Φ\Phi combines finite-support cochains for the nonnegative JnJ_n with exterior Koszul variables for the negative modes. To specify its inverse, let V(p)V^{(p)} be the cyclic smooth module whose generator is killed by JnJ_n for n≥pn\geq p, and set Tp=Φ(V(p))T_p=\Phi(V^{(p)}). A kernel-local equivalence is a map N→N′N\to N' inducing quasi-isomorphisms on every complex Hom⁡•(Tp,N)\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(T_p,N). The inverse construction is

Ψ(N)=⋃p≥0Hom⁡•(Tp,N). \Psi(N)=\bigcup_{p\geq0}\operatorname{Hom}^\bullet(T_p,N).

The field-module theorem identifies the bounded-below derived category of smooth Heisenberg modules with curved modules localized at these maps. On the curved side, bounded below means that the simultaneous kernel of the ιm\iota_m vanishes below some degree. This is an explicit equivalence with an explicit class of inverted maps.

The choice has a consequence: the ordinary exterior vacuum module, on which all ιm\iota_m and QQ vanish, becomes zero in this localization. Every map from a standard kernel to that vacuum vanishes, as the vacuum calculation proves. A different localization in which this vacuum survives is a further problem. So are an extension to the desired unbounded domain and the comparison with fusion. The existing equivalence should neither be discarded nor mistaken for those stronger conclusions.

Support, normalization and the all-jet limit

The Ramond junction supplies an independently defined support category. Fix S=ℂ[[q]]/(qℓ)S=\mathbb C[[q]]/(q^\ell) and set

A=S[x,g],P=S[x,y]⊗Λ(θ,η),Dθ=x,Dy=−η,g=−∂y. A=S[x,g],\qquad P=S[x,y]\otimes\Lambda(\theta,\eta), \qquad D\theta=x,\quad Dy=-\eta,\quad g=-\partial_y.

The supported duality theorem identifies right derived BB-modules with

D(x,g)-tor(A)={M∈D(A):M[x−1]=0=M[g−1]}, D_{(x,g)\text{-tor}}(A) =\{M\in D(A):M[x^{-1}]=0=M[g^{-1}]\},

For all jets write P∞=S[xi,yn]⊗Λ(θi,ηn)P_\infty=S[x_i,y_n]\otimes\Lambda(\theta_i,\eta_n), with i≥0i\geq0, n≥1n\geq1, and differential D=∑ixi∂θi−∑nηn∂ynD=\sum_i x_i\partial_{\theta_i}-\sum_n\eta_n\partial_{y_n}. In the independently coordinate-supported smooth category, this junction is not compact. Therefore the finite-generator proof does not establish the all-jet equivalence. On the larger full boundary-module categories there is a separate failure of generation: nonzero polynomial modules of nonnegative energy, with finite free energy pieces, have zero derived Hom from the junction. This statement retains translation and the prescribed internal-shift mapping convention. An energy bound alone does not remove those right orthogonals.

Residues supply a second distinction. For the normalized odd field CC and its physical normalization c=qCc=qC, put κi=∂θi\kappa_i=\partial_{\theta_i} and

Ω=−Res⁡zC(z)∂C(z)=∑i≥0(2i+1)ηi+1κi,ρ=q2Ω. \Omega=-\operatorname{Res}_z C(z)\partial C(z) =\sum_{i\geq0}(2i+1)\eta_{i+1}\kappa_i, \qquad \rho=q^2\Omega.

Which local maps survive passage to derived objects?

The original quartet adds conjugate fields to the two boundary actions. Its identities include a boundary-linear degree-minus-one map b0b_0 with [D,b0]=x0[D,b_0]=x_0, so the coordinate x0x_0 acts trivially in the derived boundary category. Requiring every object to admit such a quartet extension excludes the right orthogonals just described, but creates a stability problem.

Indeed, adjoining an odd variable ϵ\epsilon of degree −1-1 and internal degree (2,0)(2,0) gives the translated extension

ℰa=P∞⊗Λ(ϵ),da=D+aϵΩ. \mathcal E_a=P_\infty\otimes\Lambda(\epsilon),\qquad d_a=D+a\epsilon\Omega.

Its coefficients remain polynomial and da2=0d_a^2=0. After forgetting translation, retain x=x0x=x_0 and g=−∂y1g=-\partial_{y_1} and derive the substitution g=0g=0. The two-mode detector has cohomology eΛS(ϵ,η1)e\Lambda_S(\epsilon,\eta_1), where ee has degree −1-1, and

x[e]=−a[ϵη1e]. x[e]=-a[\epsilon\eta_1e].

This action is nonzero for every nonzero a∈Sa\in S, including nilpotent aa. Thus no full stable boundary subcategory containing P∞P_\infty and its allowed shifts can consist entirely of objects admitting the original quartet: fullness admits Ω\Omega, stability admits its extension, and that extension violates the required nullhomotopy of x0x_0. The nonexistence theorem concerns this specified full subcategory. Keeping chosen quartet structures and only quartet-linear maps gives a different positive category. Its derived end is scalar; its forgetful functor does not retain every boundary morphism. This change must be accounted for in any reconstruction claim.

Locality of maps introduces another independent test. Localize the junction to Q=P∞[x0−1]Q=P_\infty[x_0^{-1}]. Its underlying differential contracts by multiplication with θ0/x0\theta_0/x_0, so QQ is acyclic. Nevertheless the identity of QQ survives in the complex of local fields with polynomial normal symbols of bounded total degree at each coefficient of qq. Such symbols preserve P∞P_\infty; evaluating a proposed primitive on 1∈P∞1\in P_\infty and taking its scalar coefficient would give 0=10=1. The derived-invariance obstruction therefore excludes a derived mapping bifunctor that agrees with this unchanged polynomial prescription on every object or on the pair (P∞,Q)(P_\infty,Q).

The obstruction has a positive boundary. Writing Γ\Gamma for the even boundary field, the inverse field H(z)=b(z)Γ(z)−1H(z)=b(z)\Gamma(z)^{-1} on the even side is local, translation-covariant and boundary-linear, and satisfies [D,H]=1[D,H]=1. It has finite Laurent-polynomial outputs at each field coefficient, but its pole and symbol-degree bounds grow without bound through those coefficients. On the odd side, allowing these poles still cannot give a degree-minus-one primitive that strictly commutes with every odd boundary mode: the strict-linearity obstruction forces its value on 11 to vanish. A local derived comparison must therefore specify both its symbol class and how it derives boundary-linearity. Agreement at the original junction remains a possible requirement; unchanged agreement at every acyclic object does not.

Finite coefficient reduction preserves the derived end

There is a useful positive result before any geometric locality condition is imposed. Put R=ℂ[[q]]R=\mathbb C[[q]] and Sℓ=R/(qℓ)S_\ell=R/(q^\ell). Let AA be an RR-linear differential graded algebra and let P,QP,Q be arbitrary right AA-modules. A perfect scalar complex is a retract of a finite iterated extension of shifts of RR. The quotient SℓS_\ell is perfect because it has the two-term free resolution

Kℓ=R⊕Rθ,|θ|=−1,θ2=0,dθ=qℓ. K_\ell=R\oplus R\theta,\qquad |\theta|=-1,\qquad \theta^2=0,\qquad d\theta=q^\ell.

Write Aℓ=A⊗R𝕃SℓA_\ell=A\otimes_R^{\mathbb L}S_\ell and similarly for Pℓ,QℓP_\ell,Q_\ell. The finite coefficient comparison is

Sℓ⊗R𝕃RHom⁡A(P,Q)≃RHom⁡Aℓ(Pℓ,Qℓ). S_\ell\otimes_R^{\mathbb L}R\operatorname{Hom}_A(P,Q) \simeq R\operatorname{Hom}_{A_\ell}(P_\ell,Q_\ell).

No compactness or perfection of PP is needed. To see why, replace SℓS_\ell temporarily by a scalar complex VV. The evaluation map from V⊗R𝕃RHom⁡A(P,Q)V\otimes_R^{\mathbb L}R\operatorname{Hom}_A(P,Q) to RHom⁡A(P,V⊗R𝕃Q)R\operatorname{Hom}_A(P,V\otimes_R^{\mathbb L}Q) is the identity for V=RV=R. Both expressions preserve finite cones and retracts in VV, so the map is an equivalence for every perfect VV. Extension–restriction adjunction identifies its target at V=SℓV=S_\ell with the displayed Hom. The finite scalar complex, rather than a finite number of generators of PP, supplies the finiteness in this argument.

The comparison also preserves units and composition. For homogeneous module maps f,gf,g, an input pp in a free filtered resolution, and k,b,l∈Kℓk,b,l\in K_\ell, its chain formula is

Φ(f⊗k)(p⊗b)=(−1)|k||p|f(p)⊗kb,Φ(f⊗k)Φ(g⊗l)=(−1)|k||g|Φ(fg⊗kl). \Phi(f\otimes k)(p\otimes b)=(-1)^{|k||p|}f(p)\otimes kb, \qquad \Phi(f\otimes k)\Phi(g\otimes l)=(-1)^{|k||g|}\Phi(fg\otimes kl).

The second sign is exactly the multiplication sign in a tensor product of graded algebras. Finite scalar reduction consequently preserves specified action maps, their homotopies, finite support diagrams and arbitrary derived inverse limits. These are statements about genuine derived scalar extensions. They do not identify a newly imposed geometric class of local maps with the original mapping object. Nor do they extend to arbitrary scalar localization: for P=⨁n≥1R/(qn)P=\bigoplus_{n\geq1}R/(q^n), one has P[q−1]=0P[q^{-1}]=0, while the identity of PP survives in REnd⁡R(P)[q−1]R\operatorname{End}_R(P)[q^{-1}]. Every qNid⁡Pq^N\operatorname{id}_P is still nonzero on R/(qN+1)R/(q^{N+1}).

The first polar comparison retains intervening fields

The universal rational 𝔤𝔩2\mathfrak{gl}_2 vacuum gives an explicit first-order coefficient comparison. The first-order polar theorem constructs the coefficient and its two separately typed products, with identity comparison on the fixed singleton. It retains the curved differential, curvature, both vacua, reduction, biduality, spectators and every finite normal derivative. Its finite bounds come from weights: for input weights i,ji,j, multiplier pole order at most pp and coefficient of ℏε\hbar^\varepsilon, only output weights k<i+j+p+εk<i+j+p+\varepsilon can contribute to a principal part. The original two-precision question is thus answered at ℏ2=0\hbar^2=0 on this carrier; precision ℏ3=0\hbar^3=0 and arbitrary native module fusion require further constructions.

Quantum groups are operations on representations

The quantum-group branch asks how the products just constructed act on several representations at separated positions and through collision. A Hopf presentation supplies a coproduct, while a spectral exchange tells how two positioned factors are interchanged. The intrinsic formulation retains a monoidal category, translation and spectral symmetry. A geometric formulation instead asks for compatible product and cooperation on the factorization objects themselves. The comparison must identify the actual tensor products of modules, not merely a formula for an exchange ratio.

There are positive recognition and reconstruction theorems on their stated unitary and finiteness domains. There are also fixed-coproduct and fixed-presentation obstructions. Together these results suggest a theory whose invariant content is the representation system with its position-dependent operations; particular Hopf algebras can present parts of it. This is a possible formulation supported by those comparisons, not a theorem that every proposed quantum group is equivalent to every other one.

The rational current–ghost example tests the passage from a coefficient dual to this representation system. Its native finite adjunction is constructed classically and at first quantum order. The first-order polar comparison retains both ordered residues, spectators, finite normal derivatives, both vacua and biduality on its specified universal vacuum carrier. The next quantum order and the three-input compatibility remain additional equations. The higher-order failure of one fixed ghost product does not refute every admissible replacement in that larger problem. The current–ghost calculation explains which domain makes the first comparison finite.

The line’s differential graded quantum-group structure also has its own grading. Comparing it with a degree-zero spectral structure requires a common recipient and a map that explains that grading. Merely noticing different degrees proves neither equivalence nor universal incompatibility after all permitted changes. The module-tensor problem fixes the tensorator, unit, exchange and associativity maps that such a comparison must provide.

Starting from an arbitrary field algebra raises the converse problem. The intrinsic reconstruction begins with an independently specified monoidal representation category, translation, spectral symmetry and a fibre functor to vector spaces with the required finite-dimensional rigidity. Its coend is the universal object of matrix coefficients: the quotient that identifies coefficients related by a representation map. The intrinsic field theorem recovers fields from the multiplicativity of that universal family at a level strict over its presentation. A field algebra on its own does not supply all those categorical inputs.

Even in a given Hopf presentation, tensoring and dualizing modules use the actions as well as the exchange. The covariant module tensor supplies its transported level and action. For modules finite projective over the base, the dual-module construction uses the antipode and its inverse in the two transposed multiplicative actions, then reconstructs the fields with the annihilation operators of the new coactions. Evaluation and coevaluation satisfy the triangle identities on that finite domain. Extending this rigid domain to completed infinite modules, or deriving it intrinsically from an arbitrary chiral algebra, remains a separate reconstruction problem. An inverse-transpose formula for an exchange matrix does not specify those maps.

Finite current quotients construct the fibre

A presentation by internal cyclic objects can supply the fibre functor required for reconstruction. It need not restrict all currents to the augmentation-nilpotent sector. Let kk have characteristic zero, R=k[[ℏ]]R=k[[\hbar]] and Rn=R/(ℏn)R_n=R/(\hbar^n). Consider the degree-zero algebra BB on even generators vi,p,wi,pv_{i,p},w_{i,p}, with 1≤i≤31\leq i\leq3, p≥0p\geq0, and relations

Hom⁡(PJ,n,PJ′,n)={b∈BJ′⊗kRn:Jb=0}.\operatorname{Hom}(P_{J,n},P_{J',n}) =\{b\in B_{J'}\otimes_kR_n:Jb=0\}.

Tensor, dual, translation and exchange must also agree with the independently prescribed tables on probes and their relations. In this example the unit is the augmentation line, the antipode negates every generator, and

A neutral extension recovers the Heisenberg interaction

The Heisenberg example gives a reconstruction on a different, precisely specified finite domain. Fix κ∈ℂ×\kappa\in\mathbb C^\times and put α=πi/κ\alpha=\pi i/\kappa. A ground space is a vector space MM with a charge operator QMQ_M, or equivalently a module over the polynomial Hopf algebra Ach=ℂ[qch]A_{\mathrm{ch}}=\mathbb C[q_{\mathrm{ch}}], with coproduct Δqch=qch⊗1+1⊗qch\Delta q_{\mathrm{ch}}=q_{\mathrm{ch}}\otimes1+1\otimes q_{\mathrm{ch}}. The oscillator realization is

Fκ(M)=P⊗M,P=ℂ[x1,x2,…], F_\kappa(M)=P\otimes M,\qquad P=\mathbb C[x_1,x_2,\ldots],

with J−n=xnJ_{-n}=x_n, Jn=κn∂xnJ_n=\kappa n\partial_{x_n} for n>0n>0, and J0=QMJ_0=Q_M. Its admitted modules have locally nilpotent positive modes, with sufficiently large positive modes killing each state. Passing to ground states identifies their relative tensor over PP with the ordinary tensor of charge spaces, on which the charge is QM⊗1+1⊗QNQ_M\otimes1+1\otimes Q_N. The unit ground space has charge zero; its oscillator realization is PP.

On finite-dimensional charge spaces, the positive counterclockwise half-turn is the braiding

cM,N=flip⁡exp⁡(αQM⊗QN). c_{M,N}=\operatorname{flip}\,\exp(\alpha Q_M\otimes Q_N).

It detects more than scalar charges. Let NN be a two-dimensional nilpotent charge operator with Ne1=e0Ne_1=e_0 and Ne0=0Ne_0=0. Both simple constituents have charge zero, but

exp⁡(αN⊗N)=1+αN⊗N,exp⁡(2αN⊗N)=1+2αN⊗N. \exp(\alpha N\otimes N)=1+\alpha N\otimes N,\qquad \exp(2\alpha N\otimes N)=1+2\alpha N\otimes N.

The full turn is nontrivial. Replacing this extension by its two simple constituents loses the interaction. Braiding it against an arbitrary finite charge space has off-diagonal coefficient αQM\alpha Q_M, which will recover the polynomial action.

For an arbitrary algebraic charge module define its rational charge part by Rat⁡(M)={m:p(QM)m=0 for some nonzero p∈ℂ[t]}\operatorname{Rat}(M)=\{m: p(Q_M)m=0\text{ for some nonzero }p\in\mathbb C[t]\}. This is the largest submodule on which every vector lies in a finite-dimensional charge-stable space. The rational coreflection is right adjoint to inclusion of these locally finite modules and satisfies

Rat⁡(M⊗N)=Rat⁡(M)⊗Rat⁡(N). \operatorname{Rat}(M\otimes N)=\operatorname{Rat}(M)\otimes\operatorname{Rat}(N).

The equality uses algebraic tensors: their finite coefficient supports allow the tensor charge relation to impose finite-dimensional stable spaces in both factors. The functor is strong monoidal but not exact. For example, Ach↠Ach/(qch)A_{\mathrm{ch}}\twoheadrightarrow A_{\mathrm{ch}}/(q_{\mathrm{ch}}) is surjective, whereas its rational parts give 0→ℂ00\to\mathbb C_0.

The coefficient Hopf algebra of the finite-dimensional ground-state functor is the finite dual H=Ach∘H=A_{\mathrm{ch}}^\circ. Here the finite dual consists of functionals vanishing on a finite-codimensional ideal. It has the divided-jet basis

dλ,n(f)=f(n)(λ)n!,H=⨁λ∈ℂ,n≥0ℂdλ,n, d_{\lambda,n}(f)=\frac{f^{(n)}(\lambda)}{n!},\qquad H=\bigoplus_{\lambda\in\mathbb C,\ n\geq0}\mathbb C d_{\lambda,n},

Δdλ,n=∑i+j=ndλ,i⊗dλ,j,dλ,mdμ,n=(m+nm)dλ+μ,m+n,S(dλ,n)=(−1)nd−λ,n. \begin{aligned} \Delta d_{\lambda,n}&=\sum_{i+j=n}d_{\lambda,i}\otimes d_{\lambda,j},\\ d_{\lambda,m}d_{\mu,n}&=\binom{m+n}{m}d_{\lambda+\mu,m+n},\\ S(d_{\lambda,n})&=(-1)^n d_{-\lambda,n}. \end{aligned}

The unit is d0,0d_{0,0}, and the counit sends dλ,nd_{\lambda,n} to 11 for n=0n=0 and to 00 otherwise.

The coinduction comparison identifies V⊗HV\otimes H with the rational part of Hom⁡ℂ(Ach,V)\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb C}(A_{\mathrm{ch}},V) by v⊗h↦(a↦h(a)v)v\otimes h\mapsto(a\mapsto h(a)v). The full coinduction functor remains larger. For instance, the functional with values qchn↦n!q_{\mathrm{ch}}^n\mapsto n! satisfies no finite recurrence: its Hankel determinants are

det⁡((i+j)!)0≤i,j<m=∏j=0m−1(j!)2≠0. \det\bigl((i+j)!\bigr)_{0\leq i,j<m}=\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}(j!)^2\neq0.

This braiding extends to locally finite charge modules, where each vector is contained in a finite-dimensional stable space. It does not extend to all algebraic charge modules with their specified tensor. Indeed, a natural braiding on that whole category is determined on two regular modules by an invertible polynomial in two charges. Such a polynomial is constant, and the unit condition makes the braiding the flip. This ambient obstruction leaves the polynomial flat connection d+∑i<jtijdlog⁡(zi−zj)d+\sum_{i<j}t_{ij}\,d\log(z_i-z_j) meaningful on all algebraic modules, although its exponential transport needs a smaller domain.

The finite-support transport theorem preserves the native Ward operation, translation, unit, all already-defined finite composites and current descendants, and the three-channel equality on this domain. It supplies no automatic derived extension of the nonexact functor Rat\operatorname{Rat}, nor an all-collision logarithmic completion for a general nonabelian theory.

When the charge exchange has identity full turn

For the explicit finite charge category above, inverse-unitary exchange means that exchanging twice gives the identity. It is an algebraic inverse condition; it asserts no Hermitian inner product. Here the double exchange is exp⁡(2πiQM⊗QN/κ)\exp(2\pi iQ_M\otimes Q_N/\kappa). A monoidal change of presentation conjugates this operator and cannot remove its nontriviality.

Consider a full replete subcategory containing the unit and closed under finite sums, subquotients, tensor and duals. For this exchange, the classification says that identity full turn holds precisely for semisimple charges in an additive subgroup Γ⊂ℂ\Gamma\subset\mathbb C with λμ/κ∈ℤ\lambda\mu/\kappa\in\mathbb Z for all λ,μ∈Γ\lambda,\mu\in\Gamma. A nonzero nilpotent part at nonzero charge is detected by pairing with its simple quotient; at zero charge, self-tensoring detects it. Both contradict identity full turn. Conversely, diagonalization reduces the condition to the stated scalar integrality. For nonzero a∈Γa\in\Gamma, the injection b↦ab/κb\mapsto ab/\kappa into ℤ\mathbb Z shows that Γ=γℤ\Gamma=\gamma\mathbb Z, with γ2/κ\gamma^2/\kappa a nonzero integer. The zero group is also allowed. An odd integer permits a minus sign in the half-turn. None of these categories is closed under all extensions in the ambient charge category, because the neutral two-dimensional extension already violates the condition.

The finite-word theorem proves the same regularity for the iterated comparison and its inverse on every Πn\Pi^n, including repeated parameters. Descent to subquotients uses common external translation to include intertwiners occurring only at special parameters. The resulting strong monoidal equivalence

There is a small calculation that detects the triangular direction. From level classes to a coherent action

Let AA be the abelian group of translation-compatible monoidal natural automorphisms of the identity functor. Conjugation by the prescribed level classes makes it a GG-module. Comparing the two triple composites gives a normalized three-cocycle with values in AA. Its obstruction class in H3(G,A)H^3(G,A) vanishes exactly when coherent representatives exist. Here group cohomology means cocycles modulo coboundaries for the specified action. When the class vanishes, representative actions with the prescribed classes, modulo isomorphisms whose underlying functor is the identity, form a torsor under H2(G,A)H^2(G,A): the group acts freely and transitively after one such action is chosen. No continuity condition on either group is imposed.

The first-order quantum-plane exchange suggests another test: realize its inverse-transpose operation as a level of order two. The exchange formula alone is not that action. Its nilpotent coefficient ring k[ε]/(ε2)k[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2) and graded field inputs must be retained when formulating the comparison with the degree-zero, field-based criterion above.

When a coherent action has a classical presentation

Two examples distinguish the stages. The primitive-line example uses k[x]k[x] with primitive generator xx, zero Hopf translation and a parameter b∈kb\in k. There is also a full integral cyclic Yangian module, with positive, Cartan and negative actions and a free basis in every word degree over its stated parameter ring. A local nonlinear module comparison

The obstruction concerns this fixed-mode attachment and cyclic edge. The full regular unit marking survives, and no all-model obstruction follows. Centres describe specified classes of actions

The Ω-example gives several kinds of action on one state space. A centre is universal only relative to a specified category of actors and maps. The convolution centre, the ambient transverse monoid centre, a factorizing action category, a pointed action category and a category of physical bulk couplings pose different universal problems. The positive ambient constructions and the negative factorizing results are therefore compatible mathematical information.

For example, a non-equalizable parallel pair of action maps excludes a final object in the stated category. It need not exhibit two action objects with no common recipient. Nor does it automatically exclude a final physical bulk: that conclusion requires a realization functor carrying the relevant physical objects, maps and homotopies to the geometric action category, together with the obstructing diagram. The recipient comparison makes the difference between these witnesses explicit.

When representability fails, the action functor remains a mathematical object. One can compute its values on specified test actors, its mapping fibres and its composition. That alternative preserves information that a proposed single centre may fail to represent. It also makes the physical question sharper: which geometric actions arise from independently defined local bulk couplings, and which distinctions can prepared states detect? Formal ghost actions or global Ward symmetries do not answer that question simply by acting on the same boundary cohomology.

The centre acts on an entire module category

For an associative algebra AA in the specified symmetric convolution category 𝒞\mathcal C, let ℳA\mathcal M_A be its category of left modules. A 𝒞\mathcal C-linear functor commutes coherently with tensoring by every coefficient object of 𝒞\mathcal C; require it also to preserve colimits. Such endofunctors form a monoidal category under composition, with the identity functor as unit. The Morita-invariance theorem identifies the internal convolution centre with

Z⋆int(A)≃End_(Id⁡ℳA). Z^{\mathrm{int}}_\star(A) \simeq\underline{\operatorname{End}}(\operatorname{Id}_{\mathcal M_A}).

The right-hand side consists of natural operations on every module, compatible with the coefficient action. Composition of maps and composition of functors give its two compatible operations, hence its E2E_2 structure. A coefficient-linear equivalence of module categories conjugates these functors and identifies their centres, including the actions on modules.

Endomorphisms of one chosen vacuum module ask a different question. If K=kK=k is the augmentation module of A=k[x]A=k[x], then REnd⁡A(K)R\operatorname{End}_A(K) has cohomology Λ(ξ)\Lambda(\xi). The centre has cohomology k[x]⊗Λ(ξ)k[x]\otimes\Lambda(\xi) and bracket [ξ,x]=1[\xi,x]=1, as computed below. Replacing the identity functor by the vacuum discards the variable xx and changes the operation problem.

Applying Morita invariance to a Koszul transform requires its actual variance and coefficient recipient. The geometric transform above is contravariant and takes values in a pro-coefficient category; the theorem here requires a covariant equivalence linear over one specified coefficient category. Comparing centres across that transform therefore needs the corresponding opposite category, coefficient comparison and operation-preserving equivalence. Neither the geometric module theorem nor a vacuum Ext calculation by itself supplies all of these identifications.

The first coefficient of the factorization defect

For a connected coaugmented coalgebra CC on the full ordered collision carrier of a smooth curve, the ambient universal transverse monoid is ℰ(C)=[[C,C]]\mathcal E(C)=[\![C,C]\!]. It represents coherent diagonal actions. Its singleton coefficient is the internal mapping object ℰ(C)1≃Hom_X!(C1,C1)\mathcal E(C)_1\simeq\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}^!_X(C_1,C_1) for the diagonal tensor. This universal property does not assert factorization.

Let U12U_{12} be the open set of two distinct positions in the ordered collision space. The coalgebra coproduct gives

aC:ℰ(C){1,2}|U12→(ℰ(C)1⊠ℰ(C)1)|U12. a_C:\mathcal E(C)_{\{1,2\}}|_{U_{12}} \longrightarrow \bigl(\mathcal E(C)_1\boxtimes\mathcal E(C)_1\bigr)|_{U_{12}}.

The binary factorization defect is the cofiber cofib⁡(aC)\operatorname{cofib}(a_C) in the coefficient category. It vanishes exactly when this particular coproduct map is an equivalence. For the Heisenberg coalgebra at κ≠0\kappa\ne0, compute the full two-position coefficient and this map, retaining both ordered branches and all normal derivatives. Computing only singleton endomorphisms does not determine the answer. The construction before restriction must also describe how the coefficient meets the collision diagonal.

Compare this coefficient defect with the known obstructions in action spaces. Such a comparison requires a map of complexes or spaces; one cannot identify the invariants merely because both detect a failure of universality. This question also leaves intact the stronger two-object recipient problem: a non-equalizable parallel pair is a different witness.

Two sides and several roots

An ordinary calculation explains why both sides of an action matter. For an associative algebra AA, its diagonal bimodule is AA with left and right multiplication, and its derived centre is the complex RHom⁡Ae(A,A)R\operatorname{Hom}_{A^e}(A,A), where Ae=A⊗AopA^e=A\otimes A^{\mathrm{op}}. For A=k[x]A=k[x], the diagonal has the resolution

[Ae→xL−xRAe]. [A^e\xrightarrow{x_L-x_R}A^e].

The cochain insertion bracket has [ξ,x]=1[\xi,x]=1. Forgetting the right action instead gives REnd⁡A(A)=AopR\operatorname{End}_A(A)=A^{\mathrm{op}}, concentrated in degree zero; the forgetful map kills ξ\xi. For a matrix algebra A=Mn(k)A=M_n(k) the derived centre is kk. These Hochschild calculations retain the distinction between a two-sided end, a one-sided end and their higher operations.

For the chiral version, fix a connected coaugmented factorizing coalgebra CC on the full ordered collision carrier of a smooth curve over a characteristic-zero field. A marked bicomodule has two commuting coactions of CC, with every root retained in the middle factor and with the required factorization equivalences on disjoint opens. EI=RHom_ℳIbi(C)(𝕍I(C),𝕍I(C)). E_I=\underline{R\operatorname{Hom}}_{\mathcal M_I^{\mathrm{bi}}(C)} (\mathbb V_I(C),\mathbb V_I(C)).

There is a positive perfect base-change criterion. For a map of commutative differential graded algebras R→SR\to S, an associative differential graded RR-algebra BB, and a perfect BB-module PP, it gives

S⊗RREnd⁡B(P)≃REnd⁡S⊗RB(S⊗RP). S\otimes_R R\operatorname{End}_B(P) \simeq R\operatorname{End}_{S\otimes_R B}(S\otimes_R P).

To apply these results to EIE_I, the whole marked category and its restriction functors must have the stated scalar-extension presentations, compatibly with the differential modules and collision diagrams. Perfect coefficients at each fixed arity alone do not identify those functors or commute an infinite homotopy end with pullback. A collision can detect what a singleton misses

The Heisenberg vacuum calculation has cohomology Λ(ξ)\Lambda(\xi) at one root. Extend it constantly to TI=𝒪ℛI⊗Λ(ξi:i∈I)T_I=\mathcal O_{\mathscr R_I}\otimes\Lambda(\xi_i:i\in I), with zero differential, constant connection and collision map ξi↦ξα(i)\xi_i\mapsto\xi_{\alpha(i)}. A different extension with collision-supported terms is a different candidate, and the comparison with native marked endomorphisms remains necessary.

Other elementary calculations impose independent restrictions. A unital residue algebra map Mn(k)⊗Mn(k)→Mn(k)M_n(k)\otimes M_n(k)\to M_n(k) would be injective by simplicity and would send a space of dimension n4n^4 into one of dimension n2n^2; it is impossible for n>1n>1. This concerns a proposed matrix singleton, whereas the derived centre of a matrix boundary is scalar. A coefficientwise square-zero object J⊕MJ\oplus M, with constant one-dimensional MM, has rank two at separated pairs while the external square of its singleton has rank four. It is therefore not automatically a factorizing actor. Higher action-space tests require actors actually constructed in that category, such as the coherent Heisenberg actor.

The ordinary critical-affine centre supplies a further comparison. For the universal 𝔰𝔩2\mathfrak{sl}_2 algebra at level −2-2, with [h,e]=2e[h,e]=2e, [h,f]=−2f[h,f]=-2f, [e,f]=h[e,f]=h, (e,f)=1(e,f)=1 and (h,h)=2(h,h)=2, the quadratic field S=12:ef:+12:fe:+14:hh:S=\tfrac12:ef:+\tfrac12:fe:+\tfrac14:hh: is central. Its translates generate the ordinary centre freely. The affine calculation separates the direct centrality computation from the Feigin–Frenkel theorem giving exhaustiveness. Identifying this centre with degree zero of the marked candidate still needs a compatible map. Likewise, extending a root diagram from size NN to N+1N+1 may first require objects or maps; an Ext-class description becomes available only after specifying a linear deformation problem and its support. These distinctions keep the conditional construction useful without converting it into an unconditional existence theorem.

Native affine contractions retain the full chiral action

At critical level, the centre of an affine vertex algebra acts trivially by nonnegative modes. A contraction of that action should be an operator on the actual cochain complex, with a controlled continuation away from critical level. It must also fit the chiral products involving regular coefficients. These requirements distinguish a native homotopy from a choice of primitives separately at each energy.

Let 𝔤\mathfrak g be a simple complex Lie algebra with the specified invariant form and dual Coxeter number h∨h^\vee. Set R=ℂ[ϵ]R=\mathbb C[\epsilon], ℓ=ϵ−h∨\ell=\epsilon-h^\vee, and let CRC_R be the affine Chevalley–Eilenberg cochain vertex algebra with differential d=d0+ϵd1d=d_0+\epsilon d_1. Its states are the algebraic direct sum over energies. The formal group resolution EE retains joint formal zero-mode coordinates and polynomial positive-energy states. Write ϕ,Γ:CR→CR⊗E\phi,\Gamma:C_R\to C_R\otimes E for its two strict actors, PP for constant projection, and hh for their translation-linear homotopy. They satisfy

Dh+hd=Γ−ϕ,PΓ=1,[ϕ(a)λΓ(v)]=0.Dh+hd=\Gamma-\phi,\qquad P\Gamma=1,\qquad [\phi(a)_\lambda\Gamma(v)]=0.

The last identity concerns singular products. It does not say that their normally ordered product vanishes, and PP is not itself a strict vertex map.

[d,K̂a,n]=ϵΘ̂a,n,[d,Θ̂a,n]=0,Θ̂a,n|VR=ϵ−1a(n).[d,\widehat K_{a,n}]=\epsilon\widehat\Theta_{a,n},\qquad [d,\widehat\Theta_{a,n}]=0,\qquad \widehat\Theta_{a,n}|_{V_R}=\epsilon^{-1}a_{(n)}.

The state restriction follows because the degree-one correction retains an odd group variable or a function jet killed by PP. At critical level K̂\widehat K is the geometric Hamiltonian contraction on oper forms and vanishes on the marked H(𝔤)H(\mathfrak g) factor. Away from critical level it differs from the signed two-actor pairing by an explicit polynomial correction; these representatives are not identified without that correction.

Translation commutes with the construction:

K̂Ta,n=[T,K̂a,n]=−nK̂a,n−1.\widehat K_{Ta,n}=[T,\widehat K_{a,n}] =-n\widehat K_{a,n-1}.

The same identities hold for Θ̂\widehat\Theta. Replacing the lift by a+ϵya+\epsilon y changes K̂\widehat K by ϵK̂y\epsilon\widehat K_y and Θ̂\widehat\Theta by [d,K̂y][d,\widehat K_y]. A state of level degree qq and current length at most N≥1N\geq1 gives operator degree at most q+N−1q+N-1, uniformly in input energy and mode. This count includes central contractions inside dressed normal products. Their coefficient of level degree rr lies in the rrth power of the positive group-jet ideal; each even conjugate can remove at most one such factor. No energy completion or division by the level is introduced.

One projection and one module homotopy

The constant projection extends coherently to all chiral operations. HΓ=H0(1−ΓP),DHΓ+HΓD=1−ΓP,HΓΓ=PHΓ=HΓ2=0.H_\Gamma=H_0(1-\Gamma P),\qquad DH_\Gamma+H_\Gamma D=1-\Gamma P,\qquad H_\Gamma\Gamma=PH_\Gamma=H_\Gamma^2=0.

It includes all finite Laurent multipliers and corrects normal-product and singular-product defects together. Its higher components vanish when all inputs are in the unit subalgebra; vanishing after one arbitrary occupied vacuum insertion is a stronger condition.

Pull the adjoint chiral module back along the actual path from ϕ\phi to Γ\Gamma. If α\alpha is its action differential on the chiral Chevalley comodule, transfer gives

The unary parameter integral is exactly K̂\widehat K. The native affine proofs thus give a common chiral module homotopy retaining the fixed unary operators. Comparing its secondary operations with transverse products, merges and coherent units in one tower, and then proving intrinsic-centre finality, remain open.

Completed normal support has its own tensor product

βi*+βj=(i+ji)βi+j,I(E)*+I(F)≃I(Λ(E⊗R𝕃F)). \beta_i*_+\beta_j=\binom{i+j}{i}\beta_{i+j}, \qquad I(E)*_+I(F)\simeq I\bigl(\Lambda(E\otimes_R^{\mathbb L}F)\bigr).

Completion and products expose different open coefficients

The completed principal-part module consists of sums ∑m≥0amβm\sum_{m\geq0}a_m\beta_m with am∈Ra_m\in R and am→0a_m\to0 in the ℏ\hbar-adic topology. P̂R[u−1]=Q,Q=P̂R/PR≠0. \widehat P_R[u^{-1}]=Q,\qquad Q=\widehat P_R/P_R\ne0.

Both uu and ℏ\hbar act invertibly on QQ. Every derived coefficient reduction of QQ is zero, so ΛQ=0\Lambda Q=0. Thus P̂R\widehat P_R satisfies derived adic support and fails ordinary support. Taking ordinary open restriction after an infinite completion changes the gluing problem.

Scalar torsion makes a second distinction necessary. In the torsion example, complete ⨁n≥1PR/ℏnPR\bigoplus_{n\geq1}P_R/\hbar^nP_R by allowing coefficient families that have only finitely many nonzero entries modulo each ℏr\hbar^r. Call the resulting derived-complete module MM. wr=∑n≥rℏn−rβn−1(n),ℏrwr=0,ℏwr+1=wr−βr−1(r). w_r=\sum_{n\geq r}\hbar^{n-r}\beta_{n-1}^{(n)}, \qquad \hbar^rw_r=0, \qquad \hbar w_{r+1}=w_r-\beta_{r-1}^{(r)}.

Checking only ordinary quotients would miss it. This is a differential-module counterexample; its realization as a physical boundary coefficient is not asserted.

Products produce an open coefficient that survives even the special fibre. Let W=∏i≥0P̂RW=\prod_{i\geq0}\widehat P_R. Its intrinsic product in 𝒞ℏ\mathcal C_\hbar is

U=I(Rℕ)⊂W. U=I(R^{\mathbb N})\ \subset\ W.

An element of UU has, at each coefficient precision, one normal-order bound valid for every product coordinate. In WW the bound can depend on the coordinate. The diagonal element (β0,β1,…)(\beta_0,\beta_1,\ldots) already detects this difference modulo ℏ\hbar. The quotient theorem proves that LW=W/UL_W=W/U is scalar flat and derived complete, that uu is invertible on it, and that

LW/ℏLW≅∏i⨁mℂβm⨁m∏iℂβm≠0. L_W/\hbar L_W\cong \frac{\prod_i\bigoplus_m\mathbb C\beta_m} {\bigoplus_m\prod_i\mathbb C\beta_m}\ne0.

Consequently LWL_W differs from the completion quotient QQ, which has zero special fibre. The complete supported inclusion has right adjoint IKIK, and its open-restriction triangle is IK(X)→X→Λ(X[u−1])IK(X)\to X\to\Lambda(X[u^{-1}]). For X=WX=W its first term is UU and its last term is LWL_W.

This distinction is visible to probes. At the special fibre, suppose a supported right DℂD_{\mathbb C}-complex represented the inverse system of finite sums Pℂ⊕nP_{\mathbb C}^{\oplus n} on every perfect differential-module probe. Testing by DℂD_{\mathbb C} itself would recover the vector space ∏iPℂ\prod_iP_{\mathbb C}. Naturality under all left-multiplication endomorphisms of that free probe would recover its entire right DℂD_{\mathbb C}-action. The diagonal element then contradicts support. This proves the nonrealization theorem, and also excludes such a realization at every formal precision. Supported probes alone do not see LWL_W and are represented by UU. Retaining the pro-object, taking an intrinsic supported product, and representing all perfect probes therefore answer different questions. A physical reconstruction must determine which of these probes it admits.

Normal completion with its punctured marking

A completed regular coefficient need not determine the supported object from which it came. The missing information can lie in a punctured coefficient and its attaching map. Retaining that diagram gives a positive normal-completion equivalence, with actual inverse mapping spaces and a tensor comparison. The extra marking also explains why this result preserves the counterexamples to bare completion.

The category and its original completion

Let QQ be a commutative rational coefficient algebra with specified tangential derivations, and put R=Q[u1,…,ur]R=Q[u_1,\ldots,u_r]. Bounded presentations and coefficient change have precise consequences

A formal bound profile fixes pole order, weight transfer and finite matrix-degree bounds for each finite-input operation and each specified coherence cell. Require finite free scalar cells on finite weight blocks, and finite differential-module presentations of the whole collision diagram, including its actual normal relations. If every differential, support map, identity and coherence equation is a finite algebraic expression on each cell, a compatible framed system satisfying one common profile has a unique formal lift. Recognizing an independently defined native category and all its mapping spaces from this presentation is a further theorem.
